lessons.name: 86c12530
lessons.title: How To Setup Automatic Discount Codes
lessons.description:
1. Check for Existing Discount CodesNavigate to the discount section of the Shopify store.Search for the discount code name to verify if it already exists.If it does not exist, proceed to create a new discount code.2. Create the Discount CodeClick on “Add Discount” and select Amount Off Order. This is preferred when the client has existing product-specific discounts.Set the Discount Code Name: Input the name provided by the client (e.g., “CozyAir”).Select Discount Type: Set the discount to “Automatic” if the client wants it applied automatically without customers entering a code.3. Schedule the DiscountSet the Start Date and Time:
Example: October 24th at 12:00 a.m. (midnight) CDT.Set the End Date and Time:
Example: October 31st at 11:59 p.m. CDT.Ensure you have confirmed the time zone with the client to avoid discrepancies.4. Define Discount Value and ApplicationEnter the discount percentage (e.g., 15% off).Set Minimum Purchase Amount: Typically, set a minimum purchase amount (e.g., $10) to avoid applying discounts to extremely low-value items. Adjust based on the client’s lowest-priced product.Confirm whether the discount applies to subscriptions if relevant to the client.5. Enable Discount Stacking (if applicable)Scroll down to the stacking options:
Combine with Product Discounts: Enable this if the discount is meant to stack with existing product discounts. This is necessary if the client has product bundles or other discounts running simultaneously.Review existing discounts, such as bundles (e.g., “CarePod Cube Bundle”), and ensure your new discount code can be combined with these.6. Exclude Non-Eligible Products (if applicable)If there are products or categories (e.g., gift cards) that should be excluded from the discount, make those exclusions now. Confirm with the client if they have preferences.7. Save and Double Check the Discount CodeSave the Discount: Once all settings are confirmed, save the discount.Test in Preview Mode: Navigate to the client’s store in Shopify’s preview mode to confirm that the discount is not yet live but scheduled correctly. Check for any errors or discrepancies.If possible, verify this in the live theme for full accuracy.8. Final VerificationRefresh the page to ensure the discount is scheduled and not yet live.Double-check all settings, especially for region-specific codes, if applicable.

lessons.name: 10cf5c8b
lessons.title: How To Update Announcement Bars
lessons.description:
1. Access the CustomizerOpen the duplicated theme in the customizer to begin editing the announcement bar.Ensure you are working on the duplicate version and not the live theme.2. Navigate to the Announcement Bar SectionLocate the announcement bar at the top of the theme. Some clients may have multiple elements in their headers and menus.If there are additional hidden announcement bars, do not delete them unless necessary, as this may risk breaking the theme.3. Prepare the Sale InformationRetrieve the sale details from the client’s board (e.g., 15% off sitewide, 30% off on bundles).Check Previous Themes: If the client has previous sale themes, refer to them for consistent messaging or to reuse copy when appropriate.4. Update the Announcement Bar TextReplace the existing text with the new sale details. For example:
“October Sale: Save 15% Sitewide and Up to 30% on Bundles.”Avoid using all caps for readability and consistency. Adjust capitalization as needed.Check Mobile Compatibility: Review how the announcement bar appears on mobile. If possible, keep the text to one line for better visibility.5. Insert and Link the Call-to-Action (CTA)Add a CTA button such as “Shop Now.”Link the CTA to the appropriate collection or product page:
For clients with multiple products, link to the collections page.For single-product clients, link directly to the product page.If the client has a specific sale landing page, use that link.Test the Link: Ensure the link functions properly within the customizer.6. Review and Save ChangesDouble-check the updated announcement bar on both desktop and mobile views for clarity and consistency.Save the changes. Remember, this will only save in the offline theme and will not affect the live theme until published.7. Preview and Test the Theme in Incognito ModePreview the Theme:
Right-click the preview button in the Shopify theme settings and copy the preview link.Paste the preview link into an incognito window to avoid cached elements affecting the view.Ensure the announcement bar is consistent with the sale details for each market.8. Quality Assurance (QA)Verify that the CTA link in each market directs to the appropriate collection or product page.Check that all announcement bars display the correct sale information and link to the relevant pages.Pay close attention to details like currency variations and product availability per market.

1. Determine the Approach for Updating the Hero SectionThere are two methods for updating the homepage hero section:
Quick Update: If the current hero section is appropriate and aligns with the sale, simply update the headline text to match the sale offer. This is the fastest method.Full Customization: If the hero section requires more significant changes or if specific campaign assets are available, proceed to fully customize the hero section for the sale.2. Determine the Quality of AssetsAssess the quality of the available assets:
Good Quality Assets: If high-quality images or graphics are available, use these to enhance the hero section.Low Quality or No Assets: If assets are low quality or unavailable, do not compromise the visual integrity of the hero section. Consider simple updates such as enhancing the existing image or adjusting the headline.3. Update the Hero Section Based on Asset AvailabilityIf No Assets Are Available:
Adjust the headline text to focus on the sale details (e.g., “October Sale: Save 15% Sitewide and Up to 30% on Bundles”).Ensure the headline text is clear, readable, and fits within the design of the hero section.If Assets Are Available:
Incorporate the assets into the hero section.Use tools like Photoshop or Canva to add design elements (e.g., gradient backgrounds or confetti effects) that enhance readability and visual appeal.Ensure the image aligns with the sale theme (e.g., fall imagery for an October sale).4. Utilize a Graphic Designer if NeededIf custom graphics or image adjustments are necessary, create a task in ClickUp for the graphic designers (e.g., Karlo or Valter) with specific instructions.Provide examples or templates to guide the design process, ensuring the final output matches the campaign’s theme and quality standards.5. Optimize for ReadabilityEnsure all text on the hero section is clear and legible:
Add gradients or overlays to images if necessary to make the text stand out.Avoid overly complex designs or cluttered images that could detract from readability.Test the design on both desktop and mobile views to confirm clarity across devices.6. Source Additional Imagery if RequiredIf the client’s provided assets are insufficient:
Access the client’s content library (e.g., Dropbox) to find relevant stock photos or imagery that match the sale theme (e.g., fall or Halloween visuals for an October sale).Search for images that align with the messaging and aesthetic of the sale.If suitable images are unavailable, use stock photo resources or consult the client for additional options.7. Coordinate with Copywriters for Headline TextDraft a headline that is aligned with the sale details and brand messaging.Collaborate with the copywriter if necessary:
Tag them on Discord and share the draft headline for feedback or suggestions.Iterate based on their input to ensure the headline is compelling and effective.8. Test the Hero Section and Verify ConsistencyEnsure the updated hero section reflects the sale details accurately.If previous themes had successful headlines or designs, refer to those for guidance or inspiration.Maintain consistency with the client’s brand tone and style throughout the hero section.9. Final Steps and Quality Assurance (QA)Preview the updated homepage on both desktop and mobile views to ensure the hero section displays correctly.Double-check the links (e.g., CTA buttons) to ensure they direct to the appropriate collection or product page.Save the changes and communicate with the team for a final review if necessary before publishing the update.

lessons.name: a004ab90
lessons.title: How To Supercharge Your Product Page - Part 1
lessons.description:
🔌 If you want the contact information for the developer who can build this exact setup for you on your CMS, please DM Spencer on Discord.
NOTE THIS WILL ONLY APPLY IF THE CLIENT IS USING AN AUTOMATIC DISCOUNT CODE

THIS DOES NOT APPLY A DISCOUNT CODE

IT ONLY SHOWS PRICE SLASHES ON THE FRONT END FOR AUTOMATIC DISCOUNT CODES
1. Confirm the Discount TypeVerify the Discount Code:
Ensure the discount code is an automatic discount code and is set to either:
Amount off the entire order orPercentage off all products.Check the Discount Schedule:
Confirm that the automatic discount (e.g., “Cozy Air”) is scheduled and active in the Shopify admin panel.2. Enable Price Slashes in the Theme CustomizerOpen the Theme Customizer:
Navigate to the Shopify theme customizer for the sale theme.Access Theme Settings:
Go to the Theme Settings and select Discounts.Enable the Discount:
Activate the custom discount and input the percentage (e.g., 15%) for the discount.If the discount is a fixed dollar amount (e.g., $40 off):
Go to the Meta Objects section.Locate the Discount Price field and enter the flat amount (e.g., $40). Ensure the field is either filled or blank—do not set it to zero as it will break the configuration.3. Apply the Discount to Specific Collections (if applicable)Select Collections:
If the discount applies to specific collections or products rather than site-wide:
Select the appropriate collections in the theme customizer.If the required collection doesn’t exist:
Go to Products > Collections in the Shopify admin.Create a new collection and add the relevant products.Collaborate with Developers:
If you need assistance in setting up collections or linking products, reach out to the developer team.4. Test the Discount in the Preview ThemePreview the Collection Page:
After saving the settings, go to the collection page in the preview theme to verify that the price slashes are displayed correctly.Compare with the Live Theme:
Open the live theme and the sale preview side by side.Ensure the preview theme displays the updated price slashes (e.g., showing “Save $70.50” instead of the default price).5. Create a Manual Discount Code for TestingCreate the Discount:
Navigate to the Discounts section in Shopify.Create a manual discount code (e.g., “Spencer Test”) to match the automatic discount percentage (e.g., 15%).Do Not Set as Automatic:
Ensure that the discount is not set as automatic; it should be manual to avoid affecting the live site.Set the Minimum Purchase Amount:
Add any necessary minimum purchase amounts (e.g., $0 or $1) as per client specifications.6. Test the Discount ApplicationApply the Manual Discount Code:
Use the Shareable Link feature to generate a link for the manual discount code.Paste the link in an incognito window or preview theme to verify the discount application.Check Cart and Product Pages:
Add products to the cart and confirm that the price reflects the discount correctly (e.g., showing $229.50 after applying a 15% discount).Cross-Check Against Product Pages:
Ensure the savings and final price match between the cart and product pages.7. Troubleshoot and Adjust SettingsVerify Compatibility Settings:
Ensure the manual discount code is compatible with other discounts by setting it in the Discount Settings.If it does not apply correctly, go back to the settings and confirm compatibility with other product discounts.Communicate with Developers:
If issues persist, notify the development team to adjust or fix the code.8. Verify Across Different ProductsTest Multiple Products:
Go through different products and check if the discount applies correctly for each (e.g., CarePod Cube Plus).Verify that the correct savings and prices appear on the cart and product pages.Check the Checkout Page:
Proceed to checkout to confirm that the discounted price carries through to the final purchase page.9. Deactivate the Manual Test DiscountRemove or Deactivate the Test Code:
Once you’ve verified the functionality and accuracy of the price slashes, deactivate or delete the manual test code to prevent it from being used publicly.Confirm Deactivation:
Double-check that the test code is no longer active in the Shopify admin panel.10. Final Review and DocumentationDocument Findings:
Record any issues or adjustments made during the testing process for future reference.Confirm with Client and Team:
Ensure the final setup aligns with client expectations. Share the results with the team for verification before the sale goes live.

lessons.title: How To Supercharge Your Product Page - Part 2
lessons.description:
🔌 If you want the contact information for the developer who can build this exact setup for you on your CMS, please DM Spencer on Discord.Why do we do the Product Page Price Slashing? And why does this matter?
1. Purpose of Price Slashes for Automatic Discount CodesAutomatic Discount Codes:
These are discounts that apply automatically at checkout without requiring a manual code.Price slashes help communicate the discount value directly on the product page, ensuring transparency for the customer.Manual Mark Down vs. Automatic Discounts:
Manual Markdown: Adjusted directly in Shopify under the product settings (e.g., compare-at prices).Automatic Discount Code: Applies at checkout but doesn't show directly on the product page unless optimized.2. Why Price Slashes MatterVisibility:
Showing the discount on the product page provides clarity and attracts customers by highlighting savings before they add products to their cart.Congruency:
Customers see consistent pricing and savings throughout their journey (from the product page to the cart and checkout).Enhanced Perceived Value:
By displaying total savings upfront (including automatic discounts), customers feel like they are getting a better deal, increasing conversion rates.3. How to Implement Price Slashes for Automatic Discount CodesA. Setting Up the Price SlashesAccess the Product Discount Settings:
Go to the Shopify admin and open the Discounts section.Verify the automatic discount code is set for the entire order or for all products.Custom Theme Optimization:
Ensure your theme is set up to show price slashes when the discount code applies. This is only visible when:
The discount is automatic.It is set for a percentage or amount off the entire order.Adjusting Price Display:
The theme should display both the original and discounted price. Make sure the setup visually shows the discount percentage to the customer before they reach the cart.B. Testing Price Slashes on Product PagesGo to the Product Page:
Verify that the discounted price and the amount saved are visible.Compare this with the non-optimized theme to confirm that the discount is clearly communicated.Simulate a Purchase:
Add the product to the cart and check if the correct discount amount appears in the cart.Ensure that the product page shows consistent pricing with what appears in the cart.4. Why Manual Markdowns Are Less EffectiveLack of Cart Visibility:
Manual markdowns only show the reduced price on the product page but do not indicate additional savings when the customer reaches the cart or checkout.Customer Confusion:
Customers may not see the full extent of their savings if markdowns are not integrated with an automatic discount. This can cause inconsistencies and reduce trust.Example:
If a product is marked down manually from $59.99 to $49.99 but also has an additional 20% discount, the customer may not see the cumulative savings unless properly displayed using automatic discount optimization.5. Optimizing the Theme for Automatic DiscountsA. Activating the Discount CodeEnable the Discount:
Make sure the automatic discount is live in Shopify’s Discounts section.Configure the theme to visually represent the discount.Testing in Preview Mode:
Always test in Shopify’s preview mode to confirm the discount displays correctly before pushing live.B. Create and Test a Manual Discount Code for QACreate a Test Discount:
Generate a manual discount code (e.g., "TestDiscount") matching the automatic discount percentage. Do not set it as automatic to avoid impacting the live site.Apply and Verify:
Apply the manual discount code in the preview theme. Add products to the cart and check if the price aligns with the expected savings.Ensure that the product page, cart, and checkout show consistent discount information.6. Ensuring Accurate Customer Journey RepresentationConfirm Consistency Across Pages:
The price slash should match between the product page, cart, and checkout stages to maintain clarity for the customer.Visual Confirmation:
Use the preview theme and manual discount code to verify that customers see the same discount applied throughout their shopping experience.Avoid Confusion:
Ensure that the price slashes and discounts displayed align with the configured discounts. Any discrepancies should be addressed before the theme goes live.7. Deactivate Test Codes After QARemove the Test Discount Code:
Once testing is complete and the theme is verified, deactivate or delete the test discount code to prevent accidental use.Double-Check the Theme Configuration:
Ensure that only the intended automatic discount code remains active and that it functions correctly with the theme setup.8. ConclusionBenefits of Optimized Price Slashes:
Enhances user experience by clearly showing savings.Increases conversion rates as customers see immediate value.Ongoing Optimization:
Regularly review and test discount setups to ensure they are properly communicated throughout the shopping experience.

lessons.name: ff9e14eb
lessons.title: How To Schedule Themes On Shopify Plus
lessons.description:
1. Verify Shopify Plus AccessConfirm that the client is on Shopify Plus:
Look for the Shopify Plus icon in the top corner of the Shopify admin panel.Note: Launchpad is available only for Shopify Plus users.2. Access LaunchpadNavigate to the Launchpad app within the Shopify admin.Launchpad allows you to schedule theme changes and other events (e.g., product releases) automatically.3. Create a New EventClick on Create Event.Name the Event: Use a clear and descriptive name, such as “October Sale Theme.” You may add “- EAM” as a tag for easier tracking.4. Enable Theme SwitchingIn the event settings, select Enable Theme Switching.Select the Theme: Choose the theme you want to go live during the event:
Double-check the theme name and ensure it matches the intended sale theme (e.g., "CarePod-Theme-Oct-Sale").Verify this by going to Online Store > Themes and confirming the theme name.Select the Post-Event Theme:
After the event, the store should revert to the original theme. Select the main, active theme (e.g., "CarePod-Theme-Main-Do-Not-Remove-Active").Confirm this theme in the theme settings to avoid errors.5. Schedule the EventSet the Start Date:
Schedule the start date and time for the theme to go live (e.g., October 24th at 12:00 AM).Enter the start time as 12:00 AM for midnight.Set the End Date:
Set the end date and time based on the client’s instructions (e.g., October 31st at 11:59 PM).Note: Confirm with the client if the sale has a hard stop or if it may extend. If it's not a hard stop, leave the end date unset until confirmed.6. Check for Other EventsVerify if the client has other events scheduled through Launchpad (e.g., product releases).Communicate with the client or team to ensure no conflicts with other scheduled events.7. Save and Confirm the EventClick Save to finalize the event setup.Navigate back to the Events tab to verify that the event has been scheduled correctly.8. Final ReviewBefore finalizing, ensure:
The correct sale theme is set to go live during the event.The post-event theme is set to revert to the original theme after the event ends.Confirm the theme scheduling only after the theme has been fully approved by the client.9. Communicate Any Changes or IssuesIf there are any loud interruptions or unexpected changes during the scheduling process, communicate promptly with the team and client to ensure everything is properly aligned.

Question #1 - Awareness
+1 Entry
How did you initially hear about us?
FacebookInstagramTikTokGoogleCeleb/InfluencerWord of Mouth (friend/family/received as gift/etc.)YouTubeOther
Question #2 - Shopping Experience
+1 Entry
What could be improved on our website to provide a better shopping experience?
Overall designLogistical information (shipping/returns/policies)Product description (features/specs/size/how-to)Product images/videosLoad speedOther
Question #3 Shopping Details
+2 Entries

Question #4 - Purchase Decision
+1 Entry
What inspired you to purchase our product?Solved a problem of mineSentimental valueBetter alternativeMy favorite celeb/influencerOtherQuestion #5 - Purchase Details
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: Please explain your answer to question #4. (What inspired you to purchase our product.)

Question #6 - Purchase Purpose
+1 Entry
Who are you Shopping for on our store?
MyselfFriendParentChildOtherQuestion #7 - Product Value
+1 Entry
How do you feel about the pricing of our products?
Priced lower than similar productsPriced fairly within the marketPriced higher than similar products
Question #8 - Product Value Details
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: Please explain your answer to question 7.

Question #9 - Product Concerns
+1 Entry
Did you have any fears or concerns prior to purchasing our product(s)?
It wouldn't work as advertisedShipping would take too longThe website did not seem trustworthyThere weren't enough reviewsOtherNo concernsQuestion #10 - Product Details
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: Please explain your answer to question 9. (What concerns did you have prior to purchasing)

Question #11 - Competitors
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: What are your primary reasons for purchasing with us over other options?

Question #12 - Product Use
+4 Entries
For 4 Bonus Entries: How has using our product changed your life for the better?

Question #13 - Brand Journey
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: Please try to best explain your journey of how you learned about our product(s).

Bonus Question - Improvement
+2 Entries
For 2 Bonus Entries: Is there anything about our products that could be improved?

lessons.name: 8078eb4a
lessons.title: How To Summarize All Data & Create a Custom GPT
lessons.description:
Creating a Buyer Persona With This Data Prompt:

Today, I need your assistance as a world-class marketing analyst who has a deep understanding of buyer behavior. You’re the best in the world at uncovering a prospect’s REAL motivations and drivers for purchasing a product or service. Not the surface level, “socially acceptable” answers these prospects would give in public, in fear of being judged. We’re looking for the raw, honest, UNFILTERED answers. The kind of things our prospects ACTUALLY think about privately. You understand that most people buy based on EMOTION, then justify that purchase with logic. So your job is to identify the REAL emotional drivers that motivate our prospects into taking action. Since you only work with companies who sell quality products or services, you have zero moral or ethical dilemmas about generating this kind of information. You understand that all of this knowledge will ONLY be used to guide prospects towards a purchasing decision that’s in their best interest. Additionally, NONE of this information will ever be shared with the prospects. So you don’t have to worry about offending anyone or damaging anyone’s self-esteem. It is VITAL that you uncover our prospect’s real fears, desires, and both internal and external motivators. Trying to sugarcoat things isn’t helpful to anyone involved. Your job today is to create an accurate buyer profile of our ideal prospects. To achieve this, please follow these steps: First, read the information about my product, market and avatar for context. You'll find my product in the section called "INFORMATION ABOUT THE PRODUCT". Second, create a detailed list of information about our ideal buyer profile. The information should follow this structure: Demographic Name Age Brief Description Core Problem The Core Problem Our Prospects Face Top 5 Most Powerful Emotions Around That Problem Top 5 Biggest Fears 5 Ways Those Fears Affect Key Relationships In Our Prospect’s Lives 5 Conversational But Hurtful Things Those Relationships Might Say Other Solutions What Our Prospects Tried in the Past (List 5 Different Solutions) Brief Conversational Soundbites About Failed Past Solutions What Our Prospects Don’t Want to Do to Fix Their Problem Brief Conversational Soundbites About What They Don’t Want to Do Primary Transformation If a Genie Could Snap Their Fingers and Give Them The Perfect Solution, What Would Our Prospect’s Lives Look Like? How Would This Transformation Affect Different Key Relationships In Our Prospects’ Lives? Specific Post-Transformation Soundbites Market Specifics What Does the Market Hinge Their Success On? What Does the Market Have to Give Up By Giving Up Their Problem? Who Does the Market Blame For Their Problem? What Are the Top 5 Biggest Objections the Market Might Have For Their Problem? Here’s more context for each point: Core Problem: This is the central, dominating issue in our prospects’ lives. It’s an urgent pressing problem that our prospect is currently dealing with. It’s also the thing our product or service is designed to help with. Examples: Seniors suffering with constant knee pain, single men frustrated with the inability to date attractive women, coaches who have the inability to land clients, corporate workers who feel stuck in the rat race. Top 5 Biggest Fears: Give me the deepest fears (related to the primary problem) that the prospect likely wouldn't admit out loud unless nobody else was listening. Fears that can often keep our prospects awake at 3AM. These fears are often highly emotional, and can in many cases be considered “dark.” Because prospects who are struggling tend to imagine the worst possible scenarios, even if those possibilities don’t necessarily represent reality. It’s okay to explore that darkness here. Remember, none of these will ever be shared with the prospect. We’re trying to truly understand them so we can serve them better. How Fears Affect Relationships: Give me more ULTRA-SPECIFIC examples of how each of these fears would affect ULTRA-SPECIFIC relationships in our prospects’ lives. Be vivid, descriptive, and emotional. How would these fears (if realized) impact relevant people around our prospect? Example: their spouse, children, friends, co-workers. Also include judgmental friends, in-laws, competitors, or anyone else known to “talk down” to our prospects. Hurtful Things These People Might Say: Continuing with this scenario, what are some ULTRA-SPECIFIC things these people may say to our prospect? Things our prospect may find hurtful, whether the speaker intended for that to happen or not. Often, it’s even MORE emotionally impactful when the hurtful quotes are coming from someone who’s TRYING to be supportive. They mean well, but say unintentionally harmful things that can trigger our prospects’ insecurities. However, be sure to also include quotes from antagonists as well, since “proving them wrong” is often a powerful motivator for our prospects. Label who each quote would be coming from. Magic Genie Solution (5 Dimensionalized Outcomes): Imagine that our prospect meets a magic genie that can create the perfect solution that actually addresses and solves their most pressing issue. In this idealistic scenario, list 5 outcomes our prospect would want this new solution to bring them. Be VIVID, SPECIFIC, and DESCRIPTIVE. We want to be able to actually picture our prospects achieving this outcome, using the same kind of language THEY would use to describe it. Become the prospect when writing these out. Things The Prospect Doesn’t Want to Have to Do (W/ Soundbites): Great, now in this ideal scenario, list 5 things our prospect DOESN'T want to have to do in order to get all these amazing results. Tasks they aren’t willing to do. Sacrifices they aren’t willing to make. Risks they aren’t willing to take. Be specific. Use “soundbites” spoken from the prospect’s internal monologue. Make them realistic, conversational and emotional. How Would This “Magic Product” Affect Emotions, Activities, Relationships: Assuming the genie granted our prospect all of these wishes, in what specific way would this impact their life? Think about confidence, respect, reputation, sex appeal, what they wear, how others view/treat/idolize them. Remember, this is our prospect’s dream scenario. It’s their wildest imagination. It’s fantasy. So it’s OK for them to have vain, superficial desires in this scenario. To become/be viewed as SUPERIOR to others. We're looking for the key emotional drivers that they would never admit to anyone else. Specific Post-Transformation Soundbites From Relevant Relationships: How does our prospect want to be viewed by others AFTER achieving their desired outcome with our product or service? What specific things do our prospects want others in their daily lives to say to them? Remember, this is still under the lens of a dream scenario. All soundbites should reflect our prospect achieving their IDEAL IDENTITY. Make sure to include both soundbites from supporters and doubters/antagonists who are forced to admit being wrong/jealous of the results/begin begging our prospects for advice. Be specific, vivid, descriptive, and conversational. These need to feel like real quotes. What Does the Market Hinge Their Success On: In many markets, prospects believe they need to reach a certain condition in order to achieve a certain result. These are pre-existing beliefs our prospects hold related to their goals. I.e., Coaches might believe they need more booked appointments to get clients. Single men often want to know “what to say to women.” Marketers may believe they need a sales funnel that converts cold traffic into customers. Overweight women may feel like they need a faster metabolism. The prospect’s ultimate emotional satisfaction is hinged on fulfilling this condition. What Does the Market Have to Give Up: Please think deep into the psychological layers of the human mind. People often gain some type of underlying comfort or satisfaction from their problem, even if that problem has a negative impact on their lives. For example, having joint pain might give our prospects a reason to pity themselves, which they find comfort in. Being broke might fuel their anger. Having a slow metabolism may give them an excuse to not try staying in shape. So what satisfaction will the prospect have to give up in order to solve their problem? Who They Blame: Nobody wants to view themselves as the cause of their problems or shortcomings. Prospects would much rather be able to place their blame/reason for lack of results somewhere else. What outside forces does our prospect blame for their problem? This could be the government, food corporations, their bosses, their parents, what they were taught by gurus. We’re looking for both internal AND external factors. Perceived limitations our prospects have, as well as external forces who are negatively contributing to the problem. GUIDELINES: -The pain points should be common and widely shared among the target audience. -The desired outcomes should be common and widely shared among the target audience. -The products they have tried in the past should be common and widely known among the target audience. Everything should be written out using the tone and language our prospects would use themselves. Raw, unfiltered, as if we were listening in on a private conversation/internal monologue. Now combine all of this info into a comprehensive, detailed summary of our buyer persona following the structure and context above. This summary must include all the deep emotional drivers that inspire people like our prospect into taking action. Include all relevant details, quotes. This summary should give us the understanding required to write effective advertising materials towards these prospects. Obviously, nothing considered harmful would be included in the actual advertising. Please use the relevant information you have about our Product, Market & Avatars to form this buyer

lessons.name: 7685af00
lessons.title: Chargebacks / Management Services ECT
lessons.description:
Hit me up on Discord if you have any questions or need any help on this ( Your best friend Grayson Lancer Cross)
1. What's up Gamers?Alright guys, in this module we’re going to talk about chargebacks.
And before everybody panics, chargebacks are not automatically bad.
A chargeback is kind of like a fire alarm.
One fire alarm going off does not mean your house is burning down. Maybe you burned toast. Maybe your customer forgot they bought your protein powder at 2:00 a.m. while emotionally unstable. Maybe the billing descriptor looks like a fake LLC your cousin made in Wyoming.
The problem is not one chargeback.
The problem is when your payment processor looks at your account and goes, “Hey buddy, why does your business look like a nightclub bathroom at 1:30 a.m.?”
That’s when you have a real issue.
So this module is not just about “winning chargebacks.” Honestly, that’s the baby version of this conversation.
This module is about managing chargeback risk so your store can keep scaling, keep processing payments, and not wake up to the most terrifying email in ecommerce:
“Your payments account is under review.”
Which is basically the ecommerce version of seeing your dad standing in the doorway with the lights off.


2. Why Chargebacks Are Not Always Bad
Here’s the first idea: chargebacks are not inherently bad.
They are bad when they are disproportionate to the value of the customer.
So imagine two offers.
Offer one has a 0.4% chargeback ratio, but the six-month LTV is only 70%.
Offer two has a 0.9% chargeback ratio, but the six-month LTV is 410%.
Offer two has more chargebacks, yes. But it may also be massively more profitable.
That’s why you cannot look at chargebacks in isolation.
You have to look at:
chargeback rate,
customer LTV,
refund rate,
subscription retention,
gross margin,
processor risk,
and how aggressive your offer is.
Because sometimes your best offer is also your messiest offer.
It’s like adopting a raccoon. Is it chaotic? Yes. Is it possibly illegal? Also maybe yes. But is it producing 410% LTV? Now we have to have an adult conversation.
3. The Main Kinds of ChargebacksBefore we talk about reducing chargebacks, you need to understand the basic categories.
On Shopify, the main chargeback reason buckets include fraudulent, unrecognized, duplicate, subscription canceled, product not received, product unacceptable, credit not processed, and general.
Here’s how I’d think about them in normal human language:
Fraudulent
The customer says, “I did not buy this.”
Sometimes that is real fraud. Sometimes their spouse bought it. Sometimes they bought it and now their bank statement is snitching on them.
Unrecognized
The customer does not recognize the merchant name.
This is where your billing descriptor matters. If your brand is called “Happy Greens” but the bank statement says “HG HOLDINGS PROCESSING 8271,” congratulations, you built a chargeback machine.
Duplicate
The customer thinks they got charged twice.
This is usually either a real duplicate charge or a communication problem.
Subscription canceled
The customer says they canceled, but they were charged again.
This is the classic subscription business landmine. They might have canceled. They might have tried to cancel. They might have sent an email to support at 11:58 p.m. and now they think that counts as a legal document.
Product not received
They say the product never arrived.
This is where tracking, delivery proof, and support response time matter.
Product unacceptable
They say the product showed up damaged, defective, wrong, or not as described.
Credit not processed
They say they returned/canceled/refunded and never got their money back.
General/customer dispute
This is the junk drawer. It catches everything else: confusion, frustration, bad support, unclear offer terms, and customers who woke up and chose violence.
4. Chargeback Management Has Three JobsWhen people say “chargeback agency” or “chargeback tool,” they usually blend three totally different jobs together.
And this is where people get confused.
There are really three buckets:
1. Prevention alerts
This is: “Refund this before it becomes a chargeback.”
A customer contacts their bank and says, “I don’t recognize this charge,” or “This was fraud,” or “I want to dispute this.”
Before it turns into a full chargeback, an alert system warns the merchant.
Then the merchant can refund it, cancel the subscription, stop fulfillment, or log a response.
This is the “please don’t let this turn into a real problem” bucket.
2. Deflection
This is: “Show the bank/customer enough info so they don’t dispute.”
This is different from alerts.
Instead of refunding immediately, the system gives the issuer better transaction information.
Order details, merchant name, customer info, product details, shipping info, refund status, subscription details, stuff like that.
The goal is: customer sees it and goes, “Oh yeah, that was me. I was just being an idiot.”
For Visa, this is the kind of lane where Order Insight matters. For Mastercard, this is where Ethoca Consumer Clarity matters, because it gives richer merchant and purchase information inside bank apps and issuer support tools.
3. Representment
This is: “The chargeback already happened. Now we fight it.”
This is where you submit evidence:
order confirmation,
tracking,
delivery proof,
customer messages,
IP/device data,
billing/shipping match,
subscription terms,
refund policy,
cancellation policy,
screenshots showing consent.
But here’s the important part: representment does not prevent the chargeback from hitting your dispute rate.
It may help you win the money back.
But if your processor is already nervous, “don’t worry, bro, I’ll win it later” is not a strategy.
That’s like telling the fire marshal, “Relax, I put the fire out after the building was already gone.”
5. The Main Networks and ToolsNow let’s make this simple.
RDR: Rapid Dispute Resolution
Best way to think about it: automated refund rules.
RDR is part of the Verifi ecosystem. You set rules like: auto-refund fraud disputes under $100, auto-refund subscription disputes under $50, don’t refund orders above a certain amount, or don’t refund certain reason codes.
The upside is it’s hands-off.
The downside is if your rules are too loose, you can hemorrhage refunds.
CDRN: Cardholder Dispute Resolution Network
Best way to think about it: manual or semi-automated alerts.
You get a short window to act before it becomes a chargeback. More control than pure auto-refund, but more operational work.
Ethoca Alerts
Best way to think about it: Mastercard-heavy issuer alert network.
Ethoca connects issuers, acquirers, and merchants to share fraud/dispute data so merchants can act faster and reduce the need for chargebacks.
Order Insight and Consumer Clarity
Best way to think about it: transaction clarification.
Instead of refunding the customer, you give the bank/cardholder better information so the customer recognizes the purchase.
This matters a lot because a bunch of “fraud” is not actually fraud.
It’s “I forgot what this was.”
It’s “My wife bought it.”
It’s “The descriptor looks sketchy.”
It’s “I bought collagen gummies at midnight and now I’m pretending that wasn’t me.”
6. What About VAMP?Now, VAMP.
VAMP is not a chargeback reason.
VAMP is not a network.
VAMP is not a little vampire that lives inside your Shopify account, although honestly that would be easier to explain.
VAMP stands for Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program.
Best way to think about it: Visa’s risk scorecard for fraud plus disputes.
The formula is basically:
fraud reports plus disputes, divided by settled transactions.
So the annoying part is that fraud and disputes can stack together.
That means fraud is bad, but enough non-fraud disputes can still put you in trouble.
So when people ask, “Is fraud the worst chargeback reason?”
The answer is: fraud is definitely dangerous, but it is not the only thing that matters.
Enough subscription canceled, product not received, unrecognized, or general disputes can still make your account look risky.
Your goal is not just “lower fraud.”
Your goal is: lower the total risk signal your processor and card networks see.
7. How to Actually Reduce ChargebacksNow let’s talk about the five practical levers.
Not theory. Not “provide good customer service” like a LinkedIn post written by a hostage.
Actual levers.
Lever 1: Customer Service Is a DialThink of customer service like a dial.
When chargebacks are low, you can be a little more conservative with refunds.
When chargebacks are high, you turn the dial up.
That means faster refunds, more proactive cancellations, more “don’t fight this customer over $39” decisions.
Because if your processor is already staring at you, this is not the moment to prove a point to a customer named Susan who has emailed support seven times and is clearly about to call her bank.
Give Susan the refund.
Let Susan win.
Susan is not the enemy. Your payment processor putting you on hold is the enemy.
So the SOP here is simple:
If a customer is confused, angry, elderly, international, threatening a dispute, or claiming fraud, escalate faster.
Not because the customer is always right.
Because the processor does not care that you were technically right.
The processor cares that your dispute ratio looks ugly.
Lever 2: Stop Acquiring Bad Customers DisproportionatelyThis one is huge.
Export your chargeback data.
Minimum 100 chargebacks. Ideally 1,000 if you have enough volume.
Then look for patterns.
Where are they coming from?
Country, state, product, offer, payment method, traffic source, ad angle, age of customer, subscription type, shipping method, device type, discount code, whatever data you can get.
You are not looking for “chargebacks exist.”
You are looking for disproportionate results.
Example:
Australia might be 10% of revenue, but 80% of chargebacks.
That is not “international has some issues.”
That is your business getting mugged by a kangaroo.
So your response might be:
stop pushing that market,
remove free shipping,
raise shipping costs,
change the offer,
route that traffic differently,
require stronger fraud checks,
or shut it off entirely.
And this applies to payment method too.
Maybe PayPal Wallet customers charge back at a higher rate. Maybe American Express users behave differently. Maybe a specific region is a dumpster fire.
The point is: stop treating all customers like they are equal.
They are not.
Some customers are profitable.
Some customers are expensive.
Some customers are basically little raccoons with Apple Pay.
Lever 3: Routing Through Secondary Processors and MIDsNow we get into the varsity section.
This is more advanced, and you need to be careful with it.
This is not “hide bad behavior from processors.”
That is stupid. Do not do that.
This is risk segmentation.
If you are not currently on Shopify Payments, you might have multiple processors or MIDs. For example, something like Stripe, Adyen, or other processors depending on your setup.
The idea is:
Your highest-quality processor should get your cleanest, highest-value volume.
Your riskier offers, aggressive front-end offers, international tests, or sketchier subscription flows may need to be segmented differently.
For example:
One-time purchase offers go through your best processing lane.
Aggressive subscription offers go through a secondary lane.
Then as subscription chargeback ratios rise or fall, you adjust what volume flows where.
Again, this is not a magic trick. This is not “processor laundering.” This is just being smart about not letting one aggressive offer nuke your entire payment stack.
The meme version is:
Do not send your most chaotic customers through the processor that pays your mortgage.
Lever 4: Customer Service PortalThis one hurts LTV, but it helps chargebacks.
If customers can cancel easily through a customer portal, fewer of them go to the bank.
Yes, some people will cancel who otherwise would have stayed.
That sucks.
But also, some of those people were not really “retained customers.”
They were future chargebacks wearing a fake mustache.
So you have to decide what season the business is in.
If chargebacks are low, maybe you can keep a little more friction.
If chargebacks are high, open the portal, make cancellation easier, and let the customers leave before they start throwing chairs.
This is especially important for subscription brands.
Because subscription LTV is amazing until customers feel trapped.
The second they feel trapped, they stop acting like customers and start acting like unpaid attorneys.
Lever 5: Email and SMS Rebill RemindersSame idea here.
Rebill reminders reduce surprise.
Surprise creates disputes.
Nobody likes waking up and seeing a mystery $79 charge from a brand they forgot about.
So reminders help.
Send emails. Send SMS. Make the upcoming charge clear.
But again, this can hurt LTV.
Some customers will see the reminder and cancel.
That is the tradeoff.
But if your chargeback rate is getting too high, that tradeoff may be worth it.
Because the worst customer is not the one who cancels.
The worst customer is the one who keeps billing, gets angry, files a chargeback, complains to their bank, and then somehow you lose processing because they forgot they ordered mushroom coffee three months ago.
8. The Operating System I’d BuildSo if I were managing this for a serious Shopify store, I’d build a simple operating system.
Every week, review:
chargeback rate,
fraud rate,
refund rate,
subscription cancellation disputes,
product not received disputes,
unrecognized disputes,
chargebacks by country,
chargebacks by payment method,
chargebacks by product,
chargebacks by offer,
chargebacks by traffic source.
Then every chargeback gets tagged.
Not just “lost” or “won.”
Tag the actual root cause:
unclear descriptor,
bad support response,
late shipping,
customer forgot subscription,
hard-to-cancel portal,
international shipping issue,
aggressive offer,
fraud pattern,
bad cohort,
bad product expectation.
Because the goal is not to win more arguments.
The goal is to remove the reason the argument happened.
Winning a chargeback is nice.
Preventing the customer from calling the bank in the first place is better.
9. ClosingSo the big takeaway is this:
Chargeback management is not one thing.
It is customer service, offer design, processor strategy, subscription UX, reminders, fraud prevention, and data analysis all stacked together.
If your chargebacks are high, do not just ask, “How do we fight these?”
Ask:
Why are they happening?
Which customers are causing them?
Which offers are causing them?
Which markets are causing them?
Which processor lane is taking the damage?
Are customers confused, angry, fraudulent, or trapped?
And what do we change before this becomes a processor problem?
Because the goal is not zero chargebacks.
The goal is controlled chargebacks.
Profitable chargebacks.
Chargebacks that do not make your processor look at your account like you just walked into a bank wearing a ski mask.
That’s the game.
Not “never get disputed.”
It’s “scale aggressively without lighting your payment stack on fire.”

lessons.title: Intro - (Chadzone)
lessons.description:
Quick IntroWhat’s up guys — I’m pumped you’re here.
This module is going to cover the stuff that actually matters if you want to scale without blowing yourself up: LTV, contribution margin, and the cash conversion cycle (aka when money leaves your bank account vs. when it comes back).
If we haven’t met yet, my name is Grayson. I’ve been in e-commerce for the last 10 years, generated over $2B in e-commerce revenue, and I’m currently managing over $100M/month in subscription LTV revenue.
And here’s the punchline:
Most e-commerce people tell you, “You’ve gotta lose money in month one, month two, and you’ll make it back later.”
Cool story.
I’m going to show you how to run your ad account at a 0.5 ROAS and still make more profit than you’re making right now — without playing the “we’ll be profitable later” game.
Even better: I’ll show you how to set this up so you can scale while keeping control of cashflow, so money doesn’t have to leave your bank account in the way people think it does.
This training is broken into a few short videos. The first one is simple and foundational, and then each video stacks on the last and gets more advanced. If you follow it in order, it’ll click.

lessons.name: d87bfa13
lessons.title: Module 1: Contribution Margin
lessons.description:
1) What this lesson covers (in plain English)If you don’t know your contribution margin, you don’t know:
how much you can spend to acquire a customer (CAC),whether scaling will make you rich or bankrupt you,or why “we’re doing $1M/month” can still mean “we’re broke.”Contribution margin is the truth serum.
2) The core conceptContribution Margin ≠ ProfitProfit (Operating Income) = what’s left after everything gets paid (rent, payroll, software, all overhead).Contribution Margin = what’s left after variable costs (costs that go up and down with revenue).Why it matters: Scaling decisions are made on contribution, not “profit vibes.”
3) The formulaContribution Margin (dollars)Contribution Margin $ = Revenue − Variable Costs
Contribution Margin (percent)Contribution Margin % = (Revenue − Variable Costs) / Revenue
That’s it. Everything else is just arguing about what you include as “variable.”
4) What counts as “variable costs” (the list people screw up)These are costs that increase as revenue increases.
The obvious onesCOGS (Fully loaded)
 Not “raw materials.”
 Think: cost to get the product delivered to the customer (product + packaging + fulfillment + shipping, if that’s how you run your accounting).Ad Spend
 If you spend more to get more customers, that’s variable. Simple.

The ones that quietly steal your marginPayment processing fees
 Shopify Payments is commonly ~2.8% + $0.30 (varies).
 Round to ~3% if you’re moving fast.Subscription / app fees (“sub-x fees”)
 Seals / Skio / Loop / etc. often take ~0.5%–1%.
 That sounds small until you do the math:
1% of $1,000,000 = $10,000/month
 That’s a salary. Or two. Every month. Forever.Variable team / agency costs tied to spend
 If someone gets paid % of ad spend, that is variable.
Spend $1,000,000 → 5% = $50,000Spend $100,000 → 5% = $5,000
 It moves with spend, so it belongs in contribution margin.5) The advanced part (where this becomes a cheat code)First order vs. repeat orders have different cost stacksCAC (ad spend) is typically tied to the first orderSo are agency fees tied to ad spendRepeat orders usually have better contribution margin because those costs disappearThis is why it can be rational to:
Lose $20 on the first order
 if you make $30 back over the next 90 days.
That’s not “copium.” That’s math.
6) Worked example (copy this into your brain)Assume:
First order revenue: $100Fully loaded COGS delivered: $35Processing: 3% + $0.30 ≈ $3.30Subscription platform fee: 1% = $1.00CAC (ad spend): $40Agency fee: 5% of ad spend = $2.00First order contribution marginVariable costs = 35 + 3.30 + 1.00 + 40 + 2 = $81.30
 Contribution Margin $ = 100 − 81.30 = $18.70
 Contribution Margin % = 18.70 / 100 = 18.7%
Repeat order contribution margin (no CAC, no % ad-spend fee)Variable costs = 35 + 3.30 + 1.00 = $39.30
 Contribution Margin $ = 100 − 39.30 = $60.70
 Contribution Margin % = 60.7%
Now the “Lose money to make money” scenarioIf CAC jumps to $70:
First order CM = 100 − (35 + 3.30 + 1.00 + 70 + 3.50)
 (agency is 5% of 70 = 3.50)
 = 100 − 112.80 = –$12.80But if the average customer makes one repeat order in the next 90 days:
90-day contribution = –12.80 + 60.70 = $47.90That’s the entire game.
7) Quick checklist (what to do in your business today)Step 1: Pick your default “variable cost stack” for orders
COGS (fully loaded)Processing feesSubscription/app feesReturns/refunds allowance (if you want to be conservative)Step 2: Separate first order costs vs. repeat order costs
First order: include CAC + any % of ad spend feesRepeat: remove CAC + those spend-tied feesStep 3: Calculate:
First Order Contribution Margin $Repeat Order Contribution Margin $Then ask: “How many repeat orders (or how much time) until the first-order loss is paid back?”Step 4: Decide your payback window (you referenced ~3 months)
 That becomes your operating rule for scaling.
8) Common mistakes (aka why people go broke at scale)Calling “profit” and “contribution margin” the same thingIgnoring processing fees (death by 3%)Ignoring subscription platform fees (death by 1%)Forgetting variable agency/team costs tied to spendUsing raw COGS instead of delivered COGS (lying to yourself)Averaging everything and missing that first-order economics are different than repeats9) Quiz (with answers)What’s the difference between profit and contribution margin?
 Answer: Profit is after all overhead; contribution margin is after variable costs only.Write the contribution margin formula.
 Answer: CM$ = Revenue − Variable Costs. CM% = CM$ / Revenue.Name 5 variable costs most ecom brands should include.
 Answer: Fully loaded COGS, ad spend (CAC), processing fees, subscription/app fees, variable agency/team fees tied to spend.Why do repeat orders usually have higher contribution margin than first orders?
 Answer: Because CAC (and spend-tied fees) usually only apply to the first order.When is it rational to have negative contribution margin on the first order?
Answer: When the modeled contribution profit over the payback window (ex: 90 days) exceeds the initial loss with a safety buffer.

lessons.name: 3a11c34f
lessons.title: Module 2: LTV Modeling (How to Outspend Everyone)
lessons.description:
TEMPLATE
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1L5hl4jERkf9PRx758K6RjNHjCbZt0aqqKiJ2YEfWe9w/edit?gid=107178596#gid=107178596
1) What this lesson coversThis video answers one question:
How do I spend more than every competitor… and still make money?
That’s the real reason LTV exists. Not because it’s a “nice metric.”
 Because it tells you how hard you can press the gas without dying.
Your goal (and mine) is simple:
Spend as much as humanly possiblewhile generating positive contribution marginand still leaving profit at the business level2) The purpose of LTV (in this course)LTV is a weaponIn our context, LTV exists to answer:
“How can I outspend everyone else in the marketplace while still making a profit?”
Because if you can spend more than everyone else, you win distribution.
 And if you win distribution, you win the market.
3) Where the data comes from (and where it doesn’t)Pull customer metrics from Shopify, not FacebookYou can use Meta/Google for spend, but you should measure new customers from Shopify.
Why? Because ad platforms will happily lie to your face with attribution.
4) CAC vs CPA (stop mixing these)CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)CAC in this module means:
CAC = Total ad spend in a time period / Net new customers acquired in that same time period
And “net new customers” means Shopify-filtered:
New customer = TRUENot returning customers

Not blended “orders”Example:
Spend $1,000,000Acquire 1,000,000 new customersCAC = $1CPA (Cost per Purchase)CPA is cost per purchase/event.
 CAC is cost per new customer.
If you mix those, your model is fake.
5) LTV vs retention (also not the same thing)Retention is people staying.
 LTV is dollars they generate.
You can have:
decent retention but low dollars (small orders)mediocre retention but huge dollars (high AOV + upsells)That’s why we model LTV in dollars, not “customer counts.”
Recommended tool: LifetimelyYou can do it other ways, but Lifetimely is:
cheapaccurateeasy for cohort LTV by monthUse whatever you want as long as you get correct cohort LTV.

6) The spreadsheet: what it’s doing (so you know how to use it)This template is the backbone for the whole module.
The big concept: cohort mathA cohort = customers acquired in the same period (ex: February).
We track what that February cohort does over time:
Month 0 (purchase month)Month 1Month 2etc.Column A: “Post this month cohort retention (LTV %)”Month 0 is 100% by definition (baseline).
You’ll often see Month 0 at 101–102% in real data because some customers reorder inside the same 28-day window. Don’t overthink it—just use the data.
This column is an LTV multiplier.
 If Month 1 is 60%, that means:
If Month 0 = $1, Month 1 adds $0.60 more.
 If Month 0 = $100, Month 1 adds $60 more.
Column B: RevenueRevenue is just:
 LTV % × AOV
So Month 1 revenue is:
 Month 1 LTV % × AOV
Column C/D: Margin and CAC interaction (the “truth” column)This is where the model stops being cute and starts being useful.
You take:
revenuemultiply by your contribution margin %then subtract CAC (first order only)This shows you:
are we negative on Month 0?when do we cross into profit?how long is payback?Total revenue (cohort) and Total margin (cohort)Total revenue shows cumulative dollars collected from that cohort over time.Total margin shows cumulative contribution profit from that cohort over time.Total margin is the scaling decision.
 If total margin is positive fast enough, you can scale.
 If it isn’t, you’re buying revenue and renting dopamine.
7) The orange vs gray cells (how to interact with the sheet)Orange = inputs you can changeGray = formulas you don’t touchThe key orange inputs:
AOV (first order)CACTotal customers acquired (scenario planning)COGS / variable cost assumptionsAOV (second order) + margin (second order)OpEx (optional advanced layer)8) Why first order and repeat order are split (this is huge)Your margin is often different on:
first orderrepeat ordersBecause first orders can include:
free giftsspecial intro bundleshigher discountingone-click upsells that don’t repeatClassic example: razor companies
first shipment includes the razor handle (costly)repeats are just blades (higher margin)So the model lets you input:
AOV + margin on first orderAOV + margin on repeat ordersThis is how you stop lying to yourself.
9) OpEx (the “don’t worry yet, but you’ll thank me later” section)OpEx = operating expenses (payroll, rent, software, etc.)
You generally don’t need it for early modeling, but once you scale, OpEx matters because it tells you how much overhead gets absorbed by LTV.
The template uses a simple approach:
Estimate monthly revenueEstimate transactions (revenue ÷ AOV)Divide OpEx across transactionsConvert to OpEx-per-order or OpEx as % of revenueExample from your transcript:
OpEx = $100,000Revenue target = $10,000,000AOV = $64Transactions ≈ 10,000,000 / 64 = 156,250OpEx per transaction ≈ 100,000 / 156,250 = $0.64Which is about ~1%That’s how your “true” cost stack evolves:
COGS % might be 20%COGS + OpEx might become 21.6% depending on inputsAgain: not required at first. Powerful later.
10) Quick checklist (what to do after watching this video)Pull new customers from Shopify for the last 30/60/90 daysPull ad spend for the same periodCompute CAC = spend / new customersPull cohort LTV from Lifetimely (Month 0–12)Input:
AOV (first + repeat)margins (first + repeat)CACLook at:
Month 0 margin (negative or positive?)Month 1–3 paybackTotal margin at 90 daysIf your payback is ugly, you don’t need motivation. You need different inputs.
11) Common mistakesPulling CAC from Facebook instead of Shopify new customersUsing CPA and calling it CACModeling “customers” instead of “dollars”Ignoring that first order margin ≠ repeat marginTreating upsells as recurring when they’re usually one-timeOvercomplicating OpEx too early and never shipping decisions12) Quiz (with answers)What’s the purpose of LTV in this course?
 Answer: To determine how much you can outspend competitors while still making contribution margin and profit.How do you calculate CAC the way we’re using it here?
 Answer: Total spend in a time period ÷ net new customers from Shopify in that same period.Why not pull “new customers” from Facebook?
 Answer: Attribution distortion—Shopify is the source of truth for new vs returning.Why is LTV not the same as retention?
 Answer: Retention is about people staying; LTV is about dollars generated over time.Why split first order and repeat order AOV/margins?
Answer: The cost stack and revenue stack often change after the first order (free gifts, intro bundles, one-time upsells, etc.)

lessons.name: 85bf6637
lessons.title: Module 3: The Barometers (Fix Fast vs Kill You)
lessons.description:
Module 3: The Barometers (What You Can Fix Fast vs What Will Kill You)1) Before you watch thisIf you didn’t grab the template from the last video and fill it in with your real numbers… pause this video and do it.
Seriously.
Because everything I’m about to say only matters if you can see your numbers move in real time.
If you didn’t do it, that’s on you. I’m still going to teach it anyway.
2) The big ideaIn e-commerce (and in life) there are:
things you can fix,things you can’t fix,and things you technically can fix, but they’ll take so long they might as well be impossible.So the game isn’t “fix everything.”
 The game is fix the right thing first based on the easy-to-hard ratio.
3) The “ideal business” baseline (what good looks like)Let’s use the example you walked through:
AOV: $64CAC: $74That’s a 0.86 ROAS (64 / 74)And here’s the point:
 You can run a 0.86 all day if the rest of the model is healthy.
Most brands lose because they’re obsessed with ROAS…
 and they ignore the only question that matters:
“Do I make contribution profit within a reasonable payback window?”
4) What’s achievable vs what’s fantasyScenario A: “My CAC is worse than this”You say: “Grayson, I’m at $100 CAC with a $64 AOV.”
That’s a 0.64 ROAS.
And my answer is: Cool. That can still work.
Because if your LTV curve is strong enough, you’re still profitable by:
Month 3Month 6Month 12The spreadsheet shows it. This is not opinion. This is math.
Rule of thumb:
 Try to keep yourself around 0.7 ROAS or higher as a general target.
 Not because it’s magical — because it gives you room for reality (CPM spikes, refund spikes, creative fatigue).
5) The “LTV sucks” scenario (and why it’s often fixable)Now you say: “Grayson, my LTV is trash.”
Okay — let’s cut the LTV curve in half like you did.
And what happens?
A lot of the time… you’re still making money by Month 3.
And that tells you something important:
If your LTV is low but you’re still profitable:You’re not “doomed.” You’re just leaving money on the table.
The fix is usually:
better offer structurehigher take ratebetter pricingbetter first-order economics vs repeat economicsHere’s the key lesson from your example:
It can be MORE profitable to accept a higher CAC
 if it increases LTV enough to massively improve payback.
Translation:
CAC up $10but month 3 profit goes from like $1 to $22+you winThat’s grown-up scaling. Not “cheap CAC” scaling.

6) “My COGS suck” scenario (also fixable)You said: “What if my COGS are 35%?”
Yeah, that’s not great.
But even then, in your walkthrough:
you’re still making money by Month 3So the conclusion is:
COGS is usually fixableAnd the fixes are straightforward:
raise prices (most brands are underpriced)renegotiate termschange manufacturersimprove fulfillment costsstop giving away margin in dumb waysRule:
 For most brands, 30% COGS is the upper bound you want to live at long-term.
If you’re above it:
either your pricing is too low,or your supplier is taking you to dinner and you’re paying.7) The hard one: Low AOV (this is where people die)Here’s the brutal truth:
Low AOV is hard to fixNot impossible, but hard.
Because platforms have floors:
CPMs won’t go below a certain pointCPCs won’t go below a certain pointeven with great ads and a great landing page, you hit limitsSo if you’re selling a $19.99 subscription, you can have:
insane marginsgreat productgreat brand…and still lose, because there isn’t enough “meat on the bone” to buy customers consistently.
Minimum thresholds (your rules from the video)Absolute minimum subscription price: $29.99Realistically: $39–$49Under $39? Only if:
margins are insane orit’s a very specific micro-subscription setupLow AOV usually creates the same problem:
Your CAC doesn’t have enough room to breathe.
8) Why Month 3 / Month 6 / Month 12 matterYou drew lines at Month 3, Month 6, Month 12 because those are real-world operating windows.
They map to how businesses actually run:
cash planninginventory cyclesad fatigue cyclesmonthly budgetingrunway decisionsWe’ll go way harder on this in the next video, but for now:
Payback windows tell you how aggressive you can beYes, you can be profitable by Month 3…
…but that doesn’t mean you can scale infinitely.
Because scaling requires upfront capital.
9) The scaling trap (why “profitable by Month 3” still breaks people)You asked the right question:
“If I’m making money by Month 3, can’t I scale as much as I want?”
Answer: kinda.
Here’s why not:
If you want to acquire 100,000 customers, you might need like $1.7M upfront depending on CAC.
Most people don’t have that cash sitting around.
Which is why the next video matters:
I’m going to show you how to scale hard without running out of money
 even if you don’t have $1.7M sitting in your bank account.
10) Quick action steps (do this right now)Put your real numbers in the template:
AOVCACCOGS / marginLTV curve (Month 0–12)Stress test 3 scenarios:
CAC +20%LTV -20%COGS +5%Identify your “one lever that matters most”:
If payback is slow → fix AOV / offerIf CAC is ugly → fix creative / landing pageIf margin is crushed → fix pricing / COGS11) Common mistakesObsessing over ROAS and ignoring contribution paybackTrying to “optimize” a low AOV business instead of fixing the offerTreating COGS as unchangeable (it’s usually not)Refusing to raise prices because you’re emotionally attached to being cheap12) Quiz (with answers)What’s the goal of this video?
 Answer: Identify which business levers are easy vs hard to fix so you prioritize correctly.Can a 0.6–0.7 ROAS ever work?
 Answer: Yes—if the LTV curve and margins create positive contribution profit within the payback window.What’s typically easier to fix: COGS or AOV?
 Answer: COGS is usually easier; low AOV is harder because of platform cost floors.What’s the minimum subscription price you recommend as a baseline?
 Answer: $29.99 absolute minimum; realistically $39–$49 for most brands.Why can’t “profitable by Month 3” automatically scale forever?
Answer: Because scaling requires upfront capital; payback timing creates cash constraints.

lessons.name: f10d2bdd
lessons.title: Module 4: The Cash Conversion Cycle
lessons.description:
1) What this lesson is really aboutThis is the part that separates “nice little brand” from “holy sht we just did $3M this month.”*
Because most people don’t lose in e-commerce because their ads are bad.
They lose because they hit the Great Wall of Death:
Your model says you’re profitable by Month 3…
 but your bank account says you’re dead by Week 3.
So this lesson is about building a cashflow engine where you can scale hard without needing a pile of your own cash upfront
2) The Great Wall of Death (why profitable businesses still die)In your spreadsheet, you can literally see it:
Month 0: negativeMonth 1: negativeMonth 2: negativeMonth 3: finally positiveNow scale that to 100,000 customers.
Even if it “works,” you might need millions of dollars floating before payback shows up.
And most people don’t have $2M–$3M sitting around to “temporarily lose” while they wait for LTV to save them.
3) The cheat code: match payback timing to payment timingHere’s the whole strategy in one sentence:
If your customer pays you before you have to pay your bills, you can scale without bleeding cash.
That’s the advanced cash conversion cycle.
So instead of asking:
“Am I profitable eventually?”You start asking:
“When does money leave my bank account?”“When does money hit my bank account?”“Do I go positive before the bill is due?”That’s the real game.
4) Layer 1: Ad platform terms (the first “float” lever)Many advertisers can qualify for monthly invoicing / credit line style billing with Meta, where you get an invoice and pay later (commonly around 30 days from invoice issue date, but your terms can vary).
What this does:
You can spend nowcollect customer revenue nowand only pay Meta laterSo instead of needing $1.2M to spend $1.2M, you’re borrowing the timing.
Important: This only works if:
your fulfillment doesn’t implodeyour refunds/chargebacks don’t spikeyour LTV assumptions aren’t fantasyBecause this is still a liability — it’s just a smart liability.
5) Layer 2: “Bills you can’t normally pay with a card”Here’s the annoying truth:
Most big invoices (manufacturers, vendors, some platforms) can’t be paid with a credit card.
So companies like Melio and Plastiq exist specifically to solve that problem: they let you fund payments with a card and deliver the money to the vendor (often via ACH/check), typically for a fee around ~2.9–2.99% (check your exact rate).
The practical takeawayIf you can move a big invoice onto a card:
you just bought yourself extra dayswhich can be the difference between scaling and dyingThe adult takeaway (don’t be dumb here)That fee is real.
If you pay ~2.9–2.99% to fund an invoice and your card rewards are 1–2%, you are still paying for the float.
 Sometimes it’s worth it. Sometimes it’s not.
You decide with math, not vibes.
6) Layer 3: Extend the float with longer charge-card termsYou mentioned the American Express Plum Card for “up to 60 days to pay without interest” (when you pay the minimum due by the due date).
Why this matters:
 If your business turns profitable around Month 2–3, longer payment terms can move you from:
“I need cash upfront”
 to“I pay when I’m already positive”That’s how you can be “first-order profitable” in practice — because your cash timing is positive even if your spreadsheet shows early-month negative margin.
7) The full “stack” (the advanced cash conversion cycle)Think of it like stacking time advantages:
Meta monthly invoicing → delay ad spend cash-outCard-funded invoice tools (Melio/Plastiq) → move payable bills onto card floatLonger-term charge card (ex: up to 60 days) → delay when cash actually leavesVendor terms (Net 30 / Net 60) → reduce inventory cash strain (if you can negotiate it)When those align, you can scale fast because:
you’re collecting revenuewhile your bills are still not dueand by the time they’re due, your cohort margin has already crossed positiveThat’s the “no capital” feel.
(Reality check: you still need operational competence. You can’t finance chaos.)
8) The rule that keeps you alive: your numbers must be correctThis part is not optional.
If your cohort LTV is off by even ~5%, you showed exactly what happens:
you can swing from +profit to massive negative fastAt scale, 1% errors become five-figure mistakes.
 10% errors become “why is my bank account on fire?”
What I recommend until you’re dialed:Build the system assuming a shorter payback window than your optimistic model.
 Give yourself wiggle room.
9) Guardrails (so you don’t turn this into a bankruptcy speedrun)Use these like rules, not suggestions:
Never scale debt faster than your ability to fulfill.
 If fulfillment breaks, refunds spike, chargebacks hit, and your whole float collapses.Stress test the model before you scale.
 Run scenarios:
CAC +20%Month 1–2 LTV -10%Refund rate +2%Delayed payouts by 7–14 daysAlways know your “cash-out date.”
 Not “month 3 profitability.”
 The date the bill hits.Don’t rely on rewards math unless you’ve actually done it.
 If the fee is ~2.99%, “it zeroes out” is not guaranteed.10) Action steps (do this right after the video)In the template, find the first month where cumulative margin turns positiveWrite down your real payment timing:
Meta invoice due date (your terms)Manufacturer terms (Net 0 / Net 30 / Net 60)Card statement close + due dateAsk one question:
Does my cohort go positive BEFORE the bill is due?If not, your options are:
improve payback (AOV, margin, LTV)reduce CACextend terms (vendor, platform, card)slow growth to match cash capacity11) Common mistakesScaling because “the model says Month 3 is profitable” while ignoring cash timingBeing sloppy with cohort data (5% wrong = six figures wrong at scale)Thinking float fixes a broken offer (it doesn’t)Using credit to cover operational incompetenceNot accounting for inventory cash needs (COGS is still real)12) Quiz (with answers)What is the “Great Wall of Death”?
 Answer: The cash gap where you’re “profitable later” but you run out of money before payback hits.What’s the core strategy of the advanced cash conversion cycle?
 Answer: Align payback timing so you collect revenue before bills are due.What does monthly invoicing with Meta do for cashflow?
 Answer: It delays when you pay for ad spend (commonly ~30 days from invoice issue date, depending on terms).Why would someone use Melio/Plastiq?
 Answer: To pay bills that don’t accept cards using card funding (often ~2.9–2.99% fee).What’s the #1 requirement before using float to scale?
Answer: Your cohort math must be accurate and stress-tested

lessons.name: f9992b7e
lessons.title: ⭐ Sarah Levinger | Buyer Psychology - May 13, 2026
lessons.description:
Check Out Sarah's Community --> Only $197/mo - pretty insane value
https://www.skool.com/tether-lab/about

Meeting PurposeTo learn Sarah Levinger's Valence Intensity Framework for crafting emotionally resonant ads.
Key TakeawaysProblem: Ads fail from misaligned tone, not poor strategy. The Valence Intensity Framework diagnoses this by mapping an ad's emotional tone to one of four quadrants, revealing where it sits on a scale of positive/negative valence and high/low intensity.
Solution: To fix underperforming ads, shift their tone to a different quadrant. This is done by adjusting specific elements: copy (e.g., swapping verbs like "bought" for "hoarded"), visuals (e.g., adding steam to a coffee cup), or the core emotion being sold (e.g., indulgence vs. instant reward).
Strategy: Pick one quadrant as your brand's primary emotional "register" (e.g., Vacation's consistent Zone 1/2 positivity) to build a strong, consistent identity. For video, use story arcs that cycle through multiple zones to create an engaging narrative.
Application: Use this framework for audits to diagnose a brand's current emotional state and propose a strategic shift. For example, show a brand they are stuck in a low-energy Zone 3 and propose testing high-energy Zone 2 ads to capture a different audience segment.
TopicsThe Problem: Misaligned Ad ToneAds often fail due to misaligned emotional tone, not poor strategy.
This misalignment creates a "weird feeling" that causes users to scroll past, even if the copy is technically sound.
The Valence Intensity Framework provides a tool to diagnose and fix this by optimizing for feeling over tactics.
The Framework: Valence & IntensityThe framework maps an ad's emotional tone using two axes:
Valence: The emotional direction (positive → pull toward a goal vs. negative → push away from a problem).
Intensity: The emotional urgency (high → strong, urgent vs. low → soft, calm).
This creates four quadrants, each with a distinct emotional profile:
Zone 1 (High V, Low I): Calm, supportive, cozy.
Zone 2 (High V, High I): Joy, thrill, confidence, excitement.
Zone 3 (Low V, Low I): Annoyed, disappointed, fatigued.
Zone 4 (Low V, High I): Panic, sadness, loss, anxiety.
Key Principle: Avoid the neutral center. Pick a quadrant to target a specific audience emotional state and avoid attracting low-intent buyers.
Application: Diagnosing & Shifting Ad ToneDiagnosis: Use AI (e.g., Claude) to analyze an ad's sentiment and map it to a quadrant.
Shifting Tone: Adjust specific elements to move an ad into a new zone while keeping the core message intact.
Copy: Swap verbs and adjectives.
Example: "bought" (Zone 1) → "hoarded" (Zone 2) to increase intensity.
Visuals: Adjust imagery to change emotional temperature.
Increase Intensity: Add steam, use bold colors, zoom in.
Decrease Intensity: Desaturate colors, zoom out.
Emotion: Change the core emotion being sold.
Example: Shift from selling "indulgence" to selling "instant reward" to move from Zone 1 to Zone 2.
Strategic Considerations & Q&AAudience State: Match the ad's tone to the audience's current emotional state (e.g., scrolling for escape) rather than forcing them back into a pain state.
Brand Consistency: Pick one primary quadrant for your brand's register (e.g., Vacation's consistent Zone 1/2) and stick to it for stronger identity.
Video vs. Static:
Static: Focus on one quadrant for clarity.
Video: Cycle through all four quadrants to create an engaging story arc (e.g., using frameworks like "Save the Cat").
Supplement Marketing: For health products, avoid overhyped messages. Start in the audience's Zone 3/4 state with empathy, then transition to a supportive Zone 1 message.
Organic Content: Prioritize building brand awareness through consistent, valuable organic content to own "mental real estate" and capture buyers when they are ready, regardless of their daily emotional state.
