lessons.description:
Call Recording:
https://fathom.video/share/Uf9-ZCaTragVk-ZyDzocZdxrrEMLoXf3

Meeting Purpose
Weekly Q&A on e-commerce strategy, creative, and operations.
Key TakeawaysDouble down on your core avatar. Broadening too early dilutes your message and hurts performance. Scale one avatar to $1M/mo before expanding, ensuring your team has the capacity to handle it.
Ads fail from a belief gap, not a product flaw. Use the Evolve framework (new mechanisms, new info, avatar training) to build credibility and make your copy effective, even if you're not a natural writer.
Prioritize higher AOV customers. They have lower chargeback rates and higher approval rates. Use first-order discounts only for existing customers to attract a higher-quality subscriber base.
A new "Chargeback Master" module launches Friday. It covers advanced strategies like routing high-risk transactions to secondary processors (e.g., Checkout Champs) and a method to eliminate RDRs.
TopicsBrand Positioning & ScalingProblem: Amitoj's brand performance declined after broadening its target avatar to unlock more scale.
Solution: Revert to the original, successful niche avatar.
Rationale: A single, well-defined avatar can scale to $1M/mo. Broadening too soon dilutes the brand's message and hurts performance.
Problem: Hugo's brand in Sweden faces a "creative ceiling" due to a competitor with a more believable product mechanism.
Solution: Address the root cause—a belief gap—before expanding to new markets.
Rationale: Expanding to the US is a Band-Aid. The core issue is market skepticism, which requires repositioning, product R&D, or a pivot to survive.
Evolve Program UpdatesProgram Restructuring: After the "Iteration Playbook" is complete, the Evolve program will be restructured into a mini-crash course to deliver core concepts faster.
New Video: "How to Structure Insights" explains the "why" behind the avatar framework: to build customer belief.
Winning Ad Definitions: A new sheet defines winning ads by spend tier.
Data Gap: The sheet lacks data for the $100k–$500k monthly spend tier.
Incentive: Submit your winning ad data for a free review of your breakthrough ad.
Team Management & HiringHiring Editors:
Assessment: A paid, one-hour test edit using a random brand's script is recommended to avoid legal issues.
Strategy: Two viable approaches:
Cohort: Hire 5–10 freelancers for a trial, then keep the top performers.
Commitment: Conduct thorough interviews and assessments, then commit fully to the best candidate.
Training Strategists:
Hiring: EcomTalent provides driven, trainable candidates.
KPIs: Track spend, creative volume, hit rate (breakthroughs vs. winners), and time-to-ship.
Coaching Framework:
Goal: Teach the team to solve problems independently.
Method: Ask diagnostic questions to guide them to the answer, rather than just providing it.
Example: If CAC is high, ask: "What metric has fallen?" → "CTR is lower." → "How is the CTA?" → "It's weak."
Payment Processing & ChargebacksNew Module: "Chargeback Master" launches Friday night.
Topics: Shopify Payments mechanics, chargeback ratios, routing transactions, and a method to eliminate RDRs.
Strategy:
High AOV: Prioritize higher-priced customers. They have lower chargeback rates and higher approval rates.
First-Order Discounts: Use only for existing customers to pre-qualify them as high-quality subscribers.
COGS Target: Aim for a max of 20% of AOV, including processing fees.
Advanced Tactics ($100k+/mo):
Secondary Processors: Use Checkout Champs or Phoenix for aggressive offers to protect your Shopify Payments account.
MID Rotation: Rotate high-risk transactions (e.g., 3rd rebill) to different merchant accounts to isolate risk.

lessons.name: 9f277538
lessons.title: Media Buying, Operations + Open Q&A - May 20th,
lessons.description:
Call Recording:
https://fathom.video/share/Uf9-ZCaTragVk-ZyDzocZdxrrEMLoXf3

Meeting Purpose
A Q&A session on e-com strategy, media buying, and operations.
Key TakeawaysInvest in Video Editors: Hire full-time editors at $3k–$5k/month and treat them as partners. This ensures deep brand buy-in and creative ownership, which is more effective than hourly rates that incentivize slow work.
Subscription Strategy: Use high-churn, high-volume offers (e.g., 3-pack/month) to maximize short-term contribution margin for rapid growth. Transition to lower-churn models after scaling past $10M/month to build long-term LTV for an exit.
Apparel Brand Positioning: Success requires solving a clear problem. Use a unique positioning strategy (e.g., Comforts' "Essentials quality for $40") to differentiate in a crowded market.
Compliance & Brand Building: Avoid fake doctor testimonials. This tactic is unsustainable and builds a low-trust brand. Instead, use genuine authority-building methods from the Evolve Copywriting Program.
TopicsAd Performance & StrategyAd Rejection Impact: A winning ad for a supplement brand was rejected after 10 days for health claims, causing daily revenue to drop from $1.5k to $300–$400.
Solution: Make small changes (e.g., "bone loss" instead of "osteoporosis") and resubmit.
Creative Inspiration: Look beyond direct competitors for ad ideas.
Example: A clay-animated AI ad in the insurance niche was a top performer.
Rationale: Novel formats stand out and can be adapted to new niches.
Inconsistent Performance: Small-scale ad accounts (<$1k/day) will have volatile performance.
Solution: Focus on controllable inputs (creative, offers) and let campaigns run to gather sufficient data.
Tool: Use Grayson's Statistical Testing Significance Calculator to validate if performance changes are meaningful.
Compliance Check: Use Claude to pre-screen ad copy and landing pages against Meta's policies.
Team & OperationsVideo Editor Investment:
Hiring: Hire full-time editors at $3k–$5k/month. This ensures deep brand buy-in and creative ownership, unlike hourly rates that incentivize slow work.
Training: Train existing editors with Evolve's programs. To ensure engagement, require them to share weekly learnings and implementation plans in a group chat.
Co-founder Alignment:
Problem: Misaligned priorities and overlapping tasks between co-founders.
Solution: Define clear roles and KPIs. Use data to make decisions, removing emotion from debates.
Fulfillment Strategy:
Decision: Keep in-house fulfillment if it's already efficient.
Rationale: It provides cost transparency and better terms with suppliers than a combined sourcing/fulfillment agent.
Lead Time: Long lead times (4–6 weeks) are likely due to supplier delays in securing raw materials or packaging. Negotiate for better terms (e.g., 16-week terms for an 8-week lead time).
Subscription & LTVChurn vs. Growth:
Strategy: Use high-volume intro offers (e.g., 3-pack/month) to maximize short-term contribution margin for rapid growth, even if it causes high churn (~30%).
Rationale: This strategy prioritizes cash flow for scaling. Transition to lower-churn models after scaling past $10M/month to build long-term LTV for an exit.
Failed Payments:
Problem: High rate of payment failures, including "fraud suspected" (12%).
Solution: Transition from Ka-ching to Loop. Loop's superior processing is expected to increase approval rates.
Best Practice: Use a complementary product as a post-purchase upsell to increase LTV.
Apparel Brand StrategyPositioning is Key: Success requires solving a clear problem in a crowded market.
Example (Comforts): Identified a gap for a high-quality hoodie at an accessible price ($40 vs. Essentials' $140), expanding the total addressable market (TAM).
AI Creative: Use AI for B-roll and animations, but avoid AI-generated people.
Rationale: AI people can create trust issues and are less effective for building a strong brand identity.
LTV Model: Apparel brands struggle with LTV. A membership club (like Fabletics) is a viable strategy to generate consistent, high-margin revenue.

lessons.name: 80e480eb
lessons.title: How To Do Iterations + Long Q&A - May 6th, 2026
lessons.description:
Call Recording:
https://fathom.video/share/Uf9-ZCaTragVk-ZyDzocZdxrrEMLoXf3
Call Document:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AFemTf1_oI8tf-7qYtxQsYdjOip_q2fnG9C8wuoEKE4/edit?tab=t.vyawk76nop1s

Meeting Purpose
To introduce a framework for analyzing and iterating on winning ads.
Key TakeawaysDeconstruct Winning Ads: Before iterating, analyze ads using the 8-component framework: Desire, Avatar, Angle, Mechanism, Authority, Awareness Level, Emotion (Valence/Intensity), and Positioning. This reveals why an ad works, guiding effective iterations.
Iterate on Core Components: Focus iterations on the 8 components, not just formats. For example, use the "Y Train" to find deeper desires (e.g., health vs. status) or test different authority figures (e.g., a "grandpa" vs. a "son").
Empower Your Editors: Train editors in copywriting fundamentals and give them ownership of the creative process. This improves brief-to-visual congruency and can significantly boost performance, as demonstrated by Easy A Media's success.
Build Trust with Differentiation: In sophisticated markets (e.g., supplements), build trust by being factually different, not just claiming to be better. Position against competitors and use unique mechanisms or features to stand out.
TopicsThe Iteration Playbook: Deconstructing Winning AdsThe playbook provides a structured method for analyzing winning ads to understand their core drivers before iterating.
The 8 Core Components:
Desire: The customer's underlying want. Use the "Y Train" to find deeper emotional drivers (e.g., "clean washing machine" → "health hazard" vs. "social status").
Avatar: The specific person being targeted. Identify their behaviors, emotions, and demographics to make copy more specific and effective.
Angle: The specific problem the product solves.
Mechanism: The unique way the product works.
Authority: The source of credibility. Use copy to enhance authority (e.g., "one sniff" from a 30-year expert).
Awareness Level: The customer's knowledge of the problem and solutions.
Emotion (Valence & Intensity): The ad's emotional tone.
Positioning: How the product is framed against competitors, often by defining an "enemy" (e.g., "surface-level cleaners") and a unique category (e.g., "enzyme-based tablets").
Case Study: Uproot Washing Machine Cleaner AdThis ad was used to demonstrate the 8-component framework.
Desire: A clean, smell-free washing machine.
Avatar: Frustrated pet owners who have tried failed solutions (vinegar, bleach).
Angle: Fix the bad smell coming from your washing machine.
Mechanism: An enzyme-based tablet with three specific enzymes:
Alpha Amylase: Dissolves detergent film.
Protease: Breaks down keratin protein in pet hair.
Lipase: Strips grease, removing bacteria's food source.
Authority: "Grandpa," a 30-year washing machine repairman.
Awareness Level: Solution-aware (focused on failed attempts).
Emotion: Low valence, low intensity (frustrated, annoyed).
Positioning: The only enzyme-based tablet, positioned against "surface-level" cleaners.
LTV & Finance Review (Ilda's Brand)Key Metrics:
AOV: $131
Blended CAC: $48 (Meta CAC: $57)
COGS: 21% (24% with payment fees)
Profitability: The brand is highly profitable upfront, with an estimated $51 profit per customer on the first transaction.
Recommendation: Focus on backend LTV optimization. A 30-day gift card ($20–$30) is a low-cost, high-impact tactic to drive repeat purchases, as its true cost is only the COGS (~24% of face value).
Q&A: Strategy, Team Structure & TrustTeam Structure: Easy A Media's editors, trained in copywriting, now write their own scripts. This improves brief-to-visual congruency and performance.
Building Trust in Sophisticated Markets:
Be Factually Different: State unique features or facts instead of making subjective claims.
Use Positioning: Frame the product against an "enemy" and create a new category (e.g., "enzyme-based tablet").
Leverage Authority: Use credible figures or open-source practices to build belief.
Pivoting Strategy: When a problem-focused angle declines, pivot gradually. Test the new angle with a portion of creative output while maintaining the original. Create a dedicated landing page for the new angle to avoid funnel disconnects.

lessons.name: fd671670
lessons.title: Subscription Management + Open Q&A - Apr. 29, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on scaling ads, managing subscriptions, and business strategy.
Key TakeawaysAd Strategy: Fix Darius's ad structure by keeping winners active in both CBO (for scaling) and ABO (for consistent spend), as removing them from the CBO stalls its growth.
Subscription Risk: Mitigate Shopify Payments risk by diversifying with a secondary processor (e.g., Checkout Champs) and taking a Shopify Capital loan, which aligns their financial interest with yours.
Hiring Hack: Acquire small, specialized agencies ("acqui-hire") instead of hiring individuals. This provides an entire, dialed-in team for a predictable monthly cost, bypassing sales and hiring bottlenecks.
Creative Philosophy: Get customers to sell themselves by stating facts and showing, not telling. This forces engagement and makes the conclusion of superiority feel like their own discovery.
TopicsAd Campaign Structure & ScalingProblem: Darius's CBO campaign was hitting "learning limited" because winning ads were removed after being duplicated into an ABO campaign.
Solution: Keep winning ads active in both campaigns.
CBO (Testing & Scaling): Serves as the primary scaling engine.
ABO (Spend Protection): Guarantees consistent spend on proven winners, preventing them from being starved by newer, better-performing ads in the CBO.
Budgeting: Consolidate testing for multiple avatars into a single CBO at lower budgets (<$5k/day) to maximize spend for Meta's algorithm. Segment into separate campaigns only at higher scale (e.g., $50k+/day).
Subscription Risk ManagementProblem: David's supplement brand faces subscription-related chargebacks and potential Shopify Payments account suspension.
Solution:
Diversify Processors: Use a secondary processor (e.g., Checkout Champs) alongside Shopify Payments. Start with an 80/20 split and aim for 50/50.
Proactive Chargeback Mitigation:
SOPs: Create rules for immediate refunds on high-risk orders (e.g., specific card types, repeat cancellations) to prevent chargebacks.
Australia: Disable pre-checked subscriptions for this market, as its RDR (Reason Code Dispute Resolution) system makes it a high-risk region.
PayPal Wallet: Consider disabling this payment option, as it is a common source of chargebacks.
Shopify Capital Loan: Take a recurring loan to align Shopify's financial interest with yours, making an account suspension less likely.
Tip: Wait to apply for the Shopify Balance credit card until the pre-approved limit reaches its max ($250k), which typically occurs around $500k/month revenue.
Creative Strategy & CopywritingVSL Iteration: When iterating on a winning VSL, analyze the core drivers of its success (desire, angle, avatar), not just the format.
Pain Point Amplification: In copy, amplify one core pain point by showing its cascading effects (e.g., injury → missed games → lost dreams) instead of listing disconnected pains. This creates a stronger emotional connection.
Product-Aware Landing Pages: For product-aware ads, the landing page must match the audience's knowledge level. A listicle or a comparative advertorial that highlights your product's unique mechanism is often more effective than a generic problem-aware page.
"Show, Don't Tell" Marketing:
Goal: Get customers to sell themselves by letting them conclude your product is superior.
Method: State facts about competitors and your product, then let the customer draw the conclusion.
Example (CarePod): The ad simply stated it was a "stainless steel humidifier." Customers then inferred its superior cleanability and durability compared to plastic models.
Business Strategy & LogisticsAcqui-Hiring: Acquire small, specialized agencies (5–10 people) instead of hiring individuals.
Rationale: Bypasses sales and hiring bottlenecks, providing a complete, dialed-in team for a predictable monthly cost.
Leverage: As a large client, you have significant power to negotiate an acquisition.
International Expansion: Focus on the US market until reaching significant scale (e.g., $100k+/month). Fix any backend issues (e.g., chargebacks) first.
China Shipments: If a supplier suggests splitting shipments, investigate the reason. It may be a tactic to mitigate risk from under-declaring product value at customs.

lessons.name: 0612b549
lessons.title: Building for an Exit + Open Q&A - April 22nd, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on e-commerce strategy, finance, and growth.
Key TakeawaysBuild for Exit: Subscription-based brands command higher exit multiples (e.g., 7.5x EBITDA vs. 5.5x) due to predictable revenue and lower risk. Avoid being the brand's face to eliminate "key man risk."
Prioritize Experience: Accumulate experience before building a unique-product brand. Start with a simpler model to learn marketing and operations, then apply those skills to a more complex, defensible product.
Optimize Offers for LTV: A higher subscription take rate is more valuable than first-order profit. Darius's brand, profitable in 60 days, was advised to raise its non-subscription price to increase the take rate from 60% to 90%, boosting LTV by ~$18 per customer.
Scaling Requires Many Winners: At high spend ($500k+/mo), no single ad drives more than ~20% of budget. Scaling requires a portfolio of 5–15% winners, not just a few big ones.
TopicsBrand Strategy & Exit MultiplesProblem: Building a brand for exit vs. cash flow.
Solution: Prioritize experience before investing heavily in unique products.
Path 1 (Learn First): Start with a simpler product to master marketing and operations.
Path 2 (Experience First): Gain experience at an established brand (e.g., Pet Lab Co.) before launching your own.
Exit Multiples: Subscription-based brands command higher valuations.
Why: Predictable revenue and lower risk (e.g., ad account bans don't stop cash flow).
Example: A $10M EBITDA subscription brand could sell for 7.5x, while a non-subscription brand might get 5.5x.
Note: Multiples are highly dependent on EBITDA scale and market interest rates.
LTV & Offer Optimization: Darius's Brand ReviewContext: Live review of Darius's supplement brand LTV model.
Current Metrics:
AOV: $36.56
CAC: $44.53
COGS: 16.7%
Subscription Take Rate: 60%
Analysis:
Payback Period: Profitable by month 2, which is excellent.
Cash Flow: Initial loss of ~$14/customer is a cash flow issue, not a profitability issue.
Recommendation: Increase subscription take rate by raising the non-subscription price.
Goal: Increase take rate from 60% to 90%.
Impact: Boosts LTV by ~$18 per customer by month 12, far outweighing the small CAC increase.
Financing: Use Melio (2.5% fee) to pay ad spend with a credit card, bridging the cash flow gap until qualifying for Meta's net-term invoicing.
Ad Scaling & BreakthroughsBreakthrough Ad Performance:
Small Brands (<$100k/mo): A single breakthrough ad can increase total budget by 100–250% within 3 weeks.
Large Brands ($250–500k/mo): A breakthrough ad may have a slightly lower KPI (~10% lower) but still enables an 18–49% budget increase.
Scaling Principle: Scaling requires a portfolio of many winning ads, not just a few.
Why: At high spend, no single ad can sustain more than ~20% of budget without performance degrading.
Action: Focus on a system for consistently producing new winning ads.

lessons.name: 5de1ec1a
lessons.title: Strategic Ad Definitions + Open QA - Apr 16th 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on ad strategy, finance, and team structure.
Key TakeawaysAd Definitions Drive Strategy: Use new definitions (Breakthrough, Spend Winner, KPI Winner) to correctly identify winning ads. Breakthroughs (60% spend, +90% budget) enable rapid scaling, while Spend Winners (high spend, low KPI) are ripe for iteration.
Prioritize Volume Over Profitability: For subscription models, focus on acquiring high volume, even at a loss. Scale increases CAC but also lowers COGS and improves LTV, leading to higher total profit.
Match Account Structure to Scale: Simple CBOs are best for accounts under $10k/day. At higher spend, use complex structures (ABO, Zombie campaigns) to force Meta to find new pockets of demand.
Build a Scalable Creative Team: Separate media buying from creative production. A lean creative team needs ideation, briefing, and editing functions. Editors can handle briefs using AI prompts from the Evolve Copywriting Program.
TopicsAd Definitions & Scaling StrategyProblem: Teams optimize the wrong ads, wasting effort on low-spend performers.
Solution: Use new ad definitions to guide optimization and iteration.
Breakthrough Ad: Enables rapid scaling.
0–100k/mo Spend: Captures ~60% of spend and increases daily budget by 70–90%.
Spend Winner: High spend, low KPI. Meta likes the ad; the angle is strong but needs refinement.
KPI Winner: Meets KPI, low spend. Meta isn't pushing it; force budget via ABO.
Loser: None of the above.
Iteration Playbook: A future resource to guide specific actions for each ad type (e.g., add authority to a Spend Winner).
Scaling a New Store: The Native Ad TrapProblem: A new store scaled from $0 to $15k/day in 4 days, then crashed to $2k/day.
Diagnosis: The initial success was driven by native ads with fabricated stories.
Mechanism: The ads hit a "hot pocket" of the market.
Failure: The market quickly became sophisticated, recognizing the ads as fake.
Solution: Pivot to ethical, long-term creative.
Action: Analyze the initial ads to find the winning angle, avatar, and authority.
Action: Rebuild creative using the Evolve Copywriting Program principles.
Balancing AOV, CAC & LTVProblem: David's brand has a $61 AOV and $60 CAC, with a 60% gross margin.
Analysis: A monthly subscription model is more profitable than a multi-month model.
Monthly: $61 AOV, $60 CAC → -$24 loss on first order.
Multi-Month: Higher AOV ($80) and CAC ($80) → -$32 loss on first order.
Rationale: The monthly model has a faster cash conversion cycle. Even with a higher CAC ($70), it generates more profit by month two than the multi-month model.
Conclusion: Prioritize volume over immediate profitability.
Strategy: Scale the current offer until it breaks.
Rationale: Volume lowers COGS and improves LTV, making the business more profitable.
Action: Treat "buy X, get Y free" offers as an intro pack for the first order only.
Creative Team StructureProblem: Josh needs a scalable creative team structure.
Solution: Separate media buying from creative production.
Media Buyer: Manages ad account, uploads ads, analyzes data.
Junior (<$10k/day): Focus on execution.
Senior (>$10k/day): Focus on strategic testing (bid caps, new features).
Creative Team: Covers three functions:
Ideation: Generating ad concepts.
Briefing: Writing copy and creative direction.
Editing: Producing videos and statics.
Lean Model: A copywriter/strategist and an editor.
Spencer's Model: Editors write briefs using Evolve's Claude prompts, creating strong creative congruence.
Scaling Spend & CAC ProjectionsProblem: Michael needs to project CAC at higher spend levels (e.g., from $1M to $5M/month).
Analysis: CAC increases logarithmically with spend, not linearly.
Current: $90 CAC at $1M/month spend.
Projection: At $5M/month, CAC could rise to ~$140.
Rationale: This projection is based on benchmarks. Most large brands ($15M+/mo) run at a 0.7–0.9 ROAS.
Ceiling: CAC increases sharply after reaching ~70–80% of the Total Addressable Market (TAM).
Action: Use CloudCode to estimate TAM and Meta reach.
Action: Once TAM is saturated, diversify to other ad networks.

lessons.name: a1e3045b
lessons.title: Live from Marrakech Q&A - March 25th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on e-commerce strategy, ad management, and brand scaling.
Key TakeawaysAd Management: Move underperforming ads with high spend to an ABO campaign to control budget and test viability. Disable automations that kill ads based on Meta data, as it often misses true performance (e.g., NorthBeam shows a 1x ROAS is actually profitable).Brand Scaling: For distinct avatars (e.g., men vs. women), launch a separate brand. This avoids diluting the core brand's positioning and allows for a dedicated, more effective marketing strategy.Introductory Offers: Use free product (BOGO) instead of discounts for intro offers. Free product has better COGS, avoids rebill issues, and attracts higher-quality customers than discounts.Essential Automations: Implement two ad account automations to prevent catastrophic loss: 1) pause ads if spend increases 5x in 24 hours, and 2) pause ads if the URL does not equal your website.TopicsAd Management & OptimizationProblem: An ad with high spend has negative ROAS.Solution: Move the ad to a separate ABO campaign.
Rationale: This isolates the ad to control its budget and test its performance in a more controlled environment.Next Step: If it performs well, reintroduce it to the main CBO campaign.Problem: An automation kills ads that spend below KPI for a week.Solution: Disable the automation.
Rationale: Meta's data is often inaccurate. A 1x ROAS in Meta might be profitable when viewed through a third-party analytics tool like NorthBeam, which captures a more complete customer journey.Iterating on a Breakthrough AdProblem: A static ad is a breakthrough success, capturing 80% of spend.Solution: Iterate on the ad's core message and format.
Process:
Identify Core Elements: Pinpoint the ad's key angle, mechanism, authority, and avatar.Test Formats: Create new versions in different formats (e.g., video with voiceover) to see if a new medium communicates the message more effectively.Test Messaging: Rephrase the core message in new ways while communicating the same value proposition.Goal: Find new combinations of message and format that resonate with the same or a broader audience.Scaling with Multiple AvatarsProblem: A brand with a male-dominated customer base (70–80%) wants to launch a line for women.Solution: Launch a separate brand.
Rationale:
Positioning: A dedicated brand avoids diluting the core brand's identity and allows for a stronger, female-specific positioning from day one.Simplicity: Separating brands simplifies operations and marketing.Meta Ads: A separate brand allows for dedicated campaigns to target women, which is necessary as Meta's algorithm often favors male audiences.Recommendation: Start with separate landing pages and URLs under the same Shopify account to test the concept. If successful, scale into a fully independent brand.Introductory Offers & MRR StrategyFramework: Treat the first purchase as an introductory offer to onboard a customer into a monthly recurring revenue (MRR) cycle.Recommendation: Use free product (e.g., BOGO) instead of discounts for intro offers.
Rationale:
COGS: Free product is often more favorable for cost of goods sold.Rebill Cycle: Avoids complications with rebill pricing that discounts can cause.Customer Quality: Discounts tend to attract lower-quality, price-sensitive customers.Goal: Transition customers to a standard monthly subscription as quickly as possible.
Example: For a product like creatine, offer a BOGO intro offer, then guide customers to a standard monthly subscription with documentation on an increased "loading phase" dosage for the first 30 days.Kids' MRR BrandsGeneral Rule: Kids' MRR brands are difficult to sustain because parents often find them to be an extra chore.Exception: Brands solving specific, high-stakes problems for parents can succeed.
Example: Eczema supplements for kids (ages 8–18).Rationale:
High-Stakes Problem: Eczema is a significant source of self-consciousness for kids, creating a strong emotional driver for parents to find a solution.Marketing Angle: Frame the product as a solution to the child's self-consciousness, not just a health issue.Target Audience: Parents who are often frustrated with conventional medical advice.

High-Stakes Problem: Eczema is a significant source of self-consciousness for kids, creating a strong emotional driver for parents to find a solution.Marketing Angle: Frame the product as a solution to the child's self-consciousness, not just a health issue.Target Audience: Parents who are often frustrated with conventional medical advice.

lessons.name: 5e4d55b6
lessons.title: Copywriter's Checklist & Open QA - March 4th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeQ&A on media buying and a preview of the new copywriting program.
Key TakeawaysNew Scaling Protocol: Replace the "Champions Ad Set" with an ABO campaign. Duplicate winning ads into a new ABO campaign with a 10% budget of total spend to scale them independently.Copywriting Checklist: Use a 13-point checklist to improve copy quality, focusing on visual, falsifiable, and unique statements that communicate facts, not opinions.Ad Performance Diagnosis: An ad getting spend but no sales likely has a hook problem (attracting the wrong audience) or a belief problem (failing to convince the right audience).True Winners at Low Scale: At <$1k/day, a true winner will capture ~80% of the campaign budget. If this isn't happening, the ad isn't a winner yet, and more testing is needed.TopicsMedia Buying Strategy & ScalingScaling Winning Ads:
Old Method: Duplicate winners into a "Champions Ad Set" within the main CBO.New Method: Duplicate winners into a new ABO campaign.
Why: This isolates performance, preventing a single ad's failure from tanking the main CBO.Budget: Start the ABO with a budget equal to ~10% of total daily spend.Managing Volatile Winners:
Problem: A winning ad's ROAS can suddenly drop, tanking overall campaign performance.Action:
Newer Ads: Turn off immediately if performance deteriorates.Long-Term Ads: Be cautious; turning them off can sometimes do more harm than good.Alternative: Duplicate the ad to a low-budget ABO to test its viability at a smaller scale.Testing New Offers:
Method: Create a new ad set with 3-4 top-performing ads pointing to the new offer's landing page.Campaign Structure: Use a separate CBO for major offer tests (e.g., "try before you buy") to keep data clean. Minor tests (e.g., "buy 2 get 1" vs. "buy 2 get 2") can run in the main CBO.Attribution Discrepancy (CBO vs. ABO):
Problem: Ads Manager showed comparable ROAS for CBO and ABO campaigns, but a 3rd-party tool (Metrillo) showed ABO sales were 3-4x lower on a last-click basis.Insight: Meta's attribution is often first-click or view-through, while Metrillo is last-click. This explains the discrepancy and highlights the need for a robust attribution platform.Recommendation: Use Northbeam for accurate, multi-touch attribution, especially at higher spend levels.Copywriting & Creative StrategyCopywriting Checklist (13 Points):
Audience & Intent: Who is this for? Why should they care?Mechanism & Authority: What is the unique process? What makes it credible?Core Principles:
Visual: Use concrete imagery (e.g., "charging pitbull," not "optimized process").Falsifiable: State facts, not opinions (e.g., Stoli's "made in Russia" campaign).Unique: Google your headline in quotes to check for originality.Execution:
Communicate, Don't State: Let the copy imply the conclusion (e.g., "natural deodorant that performs like a toxic one").Valence & Intensity: Identify the market's emotional sweet spot (e.g., "higher valence, lower intensity" for confidence).Simplicity: Write at a 6th-grade level and condense without losing meaning.Door-to-Door Test: Would you say this face-to-face?Avoid Lecturing: Tie educational content directly to the customer's pain points.Authority in Copy:
When: Essential for shifting beliefs in sophisticated markets or for products with non-obvious mechanisms.How: Can be built through micro-creators, deep product knowledge, or social proof (e.g., "I've tried 20 air fresheners, this is the best").Mechanisms & Avatars:
A mechanism that works for one avatar may fail for another.Example: CarePod's stainless steel mechanism appeals to users seeking easy cleaning, but not to an avatar focused on aesthetics.Action: When targeting a new avatar, identify a new mechanism that resonates with their specific needs and beliefs.Ad Performance Diagnosis (Spend vs. Sales):
Problem: An ad gets significant spend but no sales.Diagnosis:
Hook Problem: The hook attracts the wrong audience, leading to high engagement but no conversions.Belief Problem: The hook attracts the right audience, but the ad fails to build belief in the claims.Action: Analyze the hook and the ad's ability to overcome audience beliefs.Creative Pod Structure:
Typical Pod: Creative Strategist + 1 Editor + 1 Graphic Designer.Scaling: Add a second editor for higher volume.Hierarchy: A Senior Creative Strategist can manage junior strategists/copywriters, who then oversee the creative team. A Senior Editor can manage the editing team.

lessons.name: 842958a1
lessons.title: Ad Strategy, Iteration &  Open QA - Feb 25th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on ad strategy, iteration, and new Evolve resources.
Key TakeawaysNew Evolve Resources: The classroom now has a new Winning Ads Doc (90+ examples), a Master Prompt Doc, and the "Overwhelmed & Stuck" video simplifying the core Learn → Research → Create → Test → Feedback Loop process.Spend Winners vs. Breakthroughs: An ad with great ad KPIs (CTR, CPC) but poor sales is a "spend winner," not a "breakthrough." Breakthroughs have ad KPIs that outperform campaign KPIs. The solution is to diagnose the funnel (hook vs. LP) and iterate.Positioning is the Key to Differentiation: Instead of directly attacking competitors, own an underserved market position. This creates a unique category and makes your product feel like the only option, driving higher one-day click ROAS.Delegate to Scale: To add new initiatives like CRO without losing ad momentum, delegate non-core tasks. Use the "Four Zones" framework (Genius, Delegate, Pleasure, Eliminate) to identify what to offload.TopicsEvolve Classroom UpdatesWinning Ads Doc: New link with 90+ examples to prevent unauthorized access.Master Prompt Doc: Centralizes all Evolve AI prompts, including those from the Alex Cooper call."Overwhelmed & Stuck" Video: Simplifies the Evolve system into a 5-step process (Learn → Research → Create → Test → Feedback Loop) to help members diagnose and fix plateaus.Evolve 3.0 Growth Guide: Details new features like a filtering system, upvoting, date tracking, and a "Breakthrough Memo" process to improve ad idea quality by requiring a clear "why" and "how."Evolve 2.0 (Mini Program): A high-level program is in development to help new members achieve a quick win and build belief in the strategy.Ad Performance & IterationProblem: An ad with high spend and strong ad KPIs (CTR, CPC) but zero sales.Diagnosis: This is a "spend winner," not a "breakthrough." Breakthroughs have ad KPIs that outperform campaign KPIs.Solution: Diagnose the funnel.
Hook Issue: The hook is strong but attracts the wrong audience or sets false expectations.Landing Page (LP) Issue: The ad's audience is mismatched with the LP's complexity.
Example: An ad for a new audience sent to an LP with 60+ options failed. A new, simplified LP with only 3 options is now being tested.Iteration Playbook (Upcoming): A new resource will provide structured iteration paths based on ad outcomes, helping isolate variables.
Framework: Analyze the ad's Angle, Mechanism, Authority, and Avatar to find what's missing or can be improved.Positioning & DifferentiationCore Principle: Positioning is how you stand out in the market. Instead of attacking competitors directly, own an underserved category.Examples:
Avis: Positioned as #2 ("We try harder") against #1 Hertz.Volkswagen Beetle: Owned the "small car" market against the "bigger is better" trend.Apple: Positioned for "creatives" against the PC's "work" image.Goal: Make your product feel like the only option.
Method: Communicate superiority without explicitly saying "we're the best."Example: "The all-natural deodorant that performs like a toxic one" implies high performance without direct comparison.Native Ads & AINative Ad Strategy: A 3-3-2 structure (3 images, 3 primary copies, 2 headlines) is recommended for testing. Each image should have a specific primary copy written for it, as Meta's breakdown tool can be unreliable.AI for Scripting: Use the Master Prompt Doc as a starting point.
Caveat: AI is a tool, not an expert. You must understand the underlying skill to analyze and improve its output.Risk: Blindly using generic prompts leads to "brain-dead" copy that is indistinguishable from competitors.Scaling & DelegationChallenge: How to add new initiatives (e.g., CRO) without losing ad momentum.Solution: Delegate non-core tasks to free up time.
Four Zones Framework:
Zone of Genius: High impact, high enjoyment. Maximize this.Delegate: High impact, low enjoyment. Delegate as soon as possible.Pleasure: Low impact, high enjoyment. Do only with spare time.Eliminate: Low impact, low enjoyment. Stop doing immediately.

lessons.name: 4bc9f999
lessons.title: Q&A + Working Harder Than Ever - Feb 11th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on e-commerce strategy, ads, and scaling.
Key TakeawaysScaling Plateaus Are Creative Plateaus: The primary bottleneck for scaling past $5k/day is a lack of new creative angles. The solution is to analyze winning ads to understand why they work and apply those patterns to new creatives.Targeting Is Creative-Driven: Meta's targeting is based on analyzing ad creative (visuals, copy, landing page), not just audience settings. To reach a specific demographic, create ads that speak directly to them.Positioning Is the Core Strategy: For saturated products, success requires a unique position based on a niche avatar or a superior mechanism. This is the foundation for a compelling offer.New Modules & Tools Are Coming: Spencer and Sean are launching new modules (copywriting, supply chain) and tools (Winning Ads GPT, Ad Review Chatbot, new ClickUp system) to support member growth.TopicsScaling & Creative PlateausProblem: A brand hit a plateau at $5k/day after scaling from $2k/day. The US market is declining while worldwide campaigns remain strong.Diagnosis: The issue is a lack of new creative angles, not the landing page.
Why: The US market is more competitive, requiring constant creative innovation.Solution: Develop pattern recognition to understand why ads work.
Process:
Analyze winning worldwide ads to identify commonalities.Bridge the gap between those patterns and current US ads.Rationale: The skill gap is in pattern recognition, which is developed through high-volume ad review and creation.Ad & Landing Page StrategyCreative Testing:
Structure: Use one CBO campaign for testing unless objectives (e.g., product, avatar) are different.Budget Allocation: Budget / Target CPA = Max Ad Sets.
Example: $1k/day budget / $50 CPA = 20 ad sets.Ad Spy Tools:
AdSpy: Essential for validating winning ads by filtering for high shares.Atria: Useful for brand research (creative mix, top LPs) but lacks share-based filtering.Landing Page (LP) Strategy:
Testing Cadence:
Iterations: 2–4 per week (with a CRO person + dev).New LPs: 1 per week (with one person).Process for New Angles:
Duplicate the highest-converting control LP.Optimize all elements (messaging, reviews, offer) for the new angle.Send traffic from relevant ads to the new LP.Low-Converting Ads:
Problem: High CTR but zero sales on a $150/day budget.Diagnosis: The ad gives interesting info but fails to create urgency or connect the problem to the product.Solution:
Niche Down: Focus on a single sub-avatar to improve conversion data for Meta.Use a Pre-Sell LP: Send traffic to an advertorial or listicle to build urgency before the product page.Test a Higher Price: A BOGO offer at a "super cheap" price can appear suspicious.Product & Brand StrategyProduct Testing:
Initial Approach: Take "big swings" with broad creative tests to find direction.Positioning: Success in saturated markets requires a unique position based on:
A niche avatar.A superior mechanism (e.g., gummy formula for a supplement).International Expansion:
Decision: If supply chain is easy, test new countries (e.g., AU/NZ) with minimal effort.Onboarding Senior Hires:
Process:
Connect with Team: Have the new hire meet with existing team members for ground-level context.Frequent Check-ins: Schedule daily or every-other-day huddles for the first week.Set Expectations: The new hire must come prepared with questions.Evolve Program UpdatesContext: Recent travel and event planning (Marrakesh) caused delayed responses.Upcoming Modules:
Wei Shaun: Supply Chain (negotiation, QC).Spencer: Copywriting.Upcoming Tools:
Winning Ads Custom GPT.Ad Review Chatbot (Apex beta first).New ClickUp System.Updated Growth Guide.

lessons.name: 38cad38b
lessons.title: In Person Q&A w/ Karlo - February 04th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeA Q&A with Spencer, Shaun, and Karlo on scaling e-com brands.
Key TakeawaysDouble Down on Winners: Focus all resources on scaling a single, proven product. Jota's brand hit $200k/mo with no strategy; applying Evolve's frameworks to this one product is the fastest path to $1M/mo.Invest in Top Talent: Hire for skill, not price. A top editor (e.g., $3–5k/mo) is a critical bottleneck, and a true strategist requires a $15–20k/mo budget.Scale Winners with ABO: To prevent CBO campaigns from starving winning ads, duplicate them into a dedicated ABO campaign. Start with a budget of ~10% of the main campaign and scale aggressively.Prioritize Benefits over Mechanisms: In ads, focus on the emotional benefit, not the scientific mechanism. Prospects care about the outcome, not the process.TopicsScaling a Winning ProductProblem: Jota's brand reached $200k/mo with a single product and no formal strategy (e.g., no customer avatar).Solution: Double down on the winner.
Focus: Improve ads, offers, and landing pages for the existing product.Team: The current structure (2 editors, 1 copywriter, 1 media buyer) is sufficient; the key is talent quality, not quantity.CRO: Add an LP agency (e.g., Arcade) to build advertorials, which are essential for scaling in the health niche.Creative Strategy & Ad PerformanceWinning Ad Definition: A "winning ad" is one that can scale, defined by:
Spend BreakthroughKPI BreakthroughBothScaling Winners with ABO:
Problem: CBO campaigns can starve winning ads of spend.Solution: Duplicate a proven winner (after 7 days at KPI) into a new, dedicated ABO campaign.Budget: Start at ~10% of the main campaign's daily budget.Rationale: This forces budget to the ad, preventing it from being outcompeted by new creatives.Axon Creative Specs:
Use 9x16 video format.Create separate, animated end cards in the Axon platform.Promo Campaigns:
Only effective for actual limited-time offers.Running back-to-back sales with the same offer trains customers to wait.RIPs (Re-purposed Ads):
Problem: Darius considered using a competitor's RIP to quickly enter a market.Solution: Create custom ads instead. Differentiation is critical for long-term success, and custom creative can be produced quickly.Team & HiringHiring Editors:
When: At $150k/mo, Mohammed should hire an editor to free up time for strategy.Investment: A top editor is a critical asset, not a commodity. Budget $3–5k/mo.Hiring Strategists:
Budget: A true e-com strategist requires a $15–20k/mo budget.Process: Hiring is sales. Use a 3-step process (Interviewer → Subject Matter Expert → Final) and ask for references.Team Learning Sessions:
Problem: Kevin's team is passive in learning calls.Solution: Make sessions interactive. Have team members prepare and present their own ad learnings to build their analytical skills and accountability.Business Focus & MindsetFocus on the Main Brand:
Problem: Mohammed splits time between a main brand and cash-flow general stores.Solution: Consolidate focus. Time is the most valuable resource. Either delegate the general stores to a VA or shut them down to accelerate the main brand's growth.Prioritize Benefits over Mechanisms:
Problem: Ernesto's ads focus on a scientific mechanism, but performance is flat.Solution: Shift focus to the emotional benefit. Prospects care about the outcome, not the process. Simplify the science or test a new brand concept.Mindset Shift:
Problem: Carlos is concerned about the minor impact of turning off underperforming ads.Solution: Focus on high-leverage activities (e.g., creating breakthrough ads) that can 10x the business, not minor media buying optimizations.Technical & Platform IssuesGoogle Ads Domain Restriction:
Problem: Ruben's entire supplement domain was restricted after one product was flagged.Solution: Isolate the issue.
Test the domain: Run a low-spend ad to a simple page on the domain to confirm it's the source of the flag.Test a new LP: If the domain is the issue, use a new landing page on a different subdomain.Appeal: If the products are compliant, appeal the decision with Google support.One-Time Purchase Products:
Problem: Mohammed sells a product with no repeat purchase potential.Solution: Build long-term value through:
Word-of-Mouth: Create an exceptional product that customers recommend.Product Line Expansion: Launch complementary products under the same brand (e.g., Ridge Wallet).

lessons.name: 01ef3e10
lessons.title: In Person Q&A - January 28th, 2026
lessons.description:
Call Starts 3:15

Meeting Purpose
Weekly Q&A on e-commerce growth strategies and challenges.
Key TakeawaysSubscriptions require a long-term view. Accept a front-end CVR dip for a 3–4x increase in 90-day LGP. Use different KPIs (e.g., break-even for subs vs. profitable for one-time purchases) to manage cash flow.Deep ad analysis is critical. Move beyond surface-level observations (e.g., "the person is older") to understand the core psychological drivers: how the ad builds credibility, creates curiosity, and shifts beliefs.For high-friction products, focus on creative. A $2.50 Revenue Per Session (RPS) is a strong metric, indicating the primary bottleneck is ad performance (e.g., driving down a $1.20 CPC), not the on-site conversion rate.Use personalized Loom videos for agency outreach. This high-intent method provides direct value and helps build trust, especially when lacking a large portfolio.TopicsAd Analysis & Learning FrameworkProblem: Surface-level ad analysis (e.g., "the person is older") fails to identify the true drivers of success.Solution: A deep analysis framework to extract transferable learnings:
Avatar: Who is the ad speaking to?Positioning: How is the product framed for that avatar?Mechanism: What core belief does the ad create?Psychological Drivers:
Credibility: How is authority built?Curiosity: What makes the viewer want to watch or read more?Storytelling: What archetype is used (e.g., Hero's Journey)?Application: Once a winning angle is identified, test it across various formats (image, VSL) and styles (us vs. them, native ads).Scaling a Supplement BrandContext: A supplement brand is hitting diminishing returns with its current Facebook-only, one-time purchase funnel.Immediate Actions:
Expand Channels: Re-engage TikTok ads, where the brand has prior success.Test Pre-landers: Create dedicated landing pages for existing winning ad messaging.Subscription Strategy:
Rationale: Subscriptions can increase 90-day Lifetime Gross Profit (LGP) by 3–4x.Trade-off: Accept a front-end conversion rate (CVR) dip (e.g., 3% → 2%) for higher long-term LGP.KPI Management: Use different KPIs for subscription vs. one-time purchase campaigns.
Subscriptions: Can run at break-even or a loss, betting on LTV.One-Time: Aim for first-order profitability.Execution: First, lab-test the product to ensure quality and customer satisfaction before launching a subscription.High-Friction Product StrategyContext: A custom jeans brand with a high-friction process (post-purchase mobile body scan).Metrics:
CVR: ~1%AOV: $250CPC: ~$1.20Analysis: The $2.50 Revenue Per Session (RPS) is strong, indicating the primary bottleneck is ad performance, not the on-site experience.Recommendation: Focus on creative to drive down the CPC and increase ad intent.
Copywriting: Use metaphors (e.g., "a tailor in your phone") to simplify the process.Avatar-Specific Ads: Target pain points like "jeans never fit me right."Landing Pages: Use listicle-style pre-landers to educate users on the 3-step process.Digital Subscription OfferContext: A fitness brand's digital subscription offer (app, gift card, shipping perks) is underperforming.Recommendation: Study Fabletics' model, which uses a deep first-order discount to drive sign-ups, then profits on the recurring subscription.Opportunity: Add a community component (e.g., on Skool) to increase value and retention.Agency Outreach StrategyContext: An agency owner needs to build trust and acquire clients without a large portfolio.Recommendation: Use personalized Loom videos for outreach.
Process: Scrape Shopify brands (e.g., with Seamless.ai), analyze their ad libraries, and record a custom Loom for each.Messaging: Tailor the message to the brand's ad volume.
High Volume (>50 ads): Focus on improving ad intent.Low Volume (<50 ads): Focus on increasing ad volume.Execution: Send 5–10 Loom videos or DMs daily to build momentum.Creator & Affiliate ProgramContext: Building a large creator program for ad content.Payment Structure:
Performance-Based: 10% of ad spend or revenue.Tiered: The percentage decreases as spend scales (e.g., 10% on first $10k, then 5%).Cap: Set a maximum payment per creator to manage costs.Acquisition Strategy:
Paid Ads: Run ads (e.g., from whitelisted creator profiles) offering a discount (e.g., 40%) to new brand ambassadors who sign up via a form.Software: Use a tool like TRIBE to manage payouts and reporting, but be aware of the 1.5% fee.Operational & Compliance IssuesCompliance (Supplements): Consult a compliance lawyer (Rob was recommended) for all FDA/FTC marketing claims.Subscription Billing: For multi-unit front-end offers, use a tool like Loop to confirm the subscription quantity and allow customers to adjust it before the first rebill.Currency Conversion (Canada → US): Use a Wise Business account to avoid high bank fees.
Setup: Create a USD "jar" within the Wise account.Process: Direct Shopify Payments to the Wise USD account → convert USD to CAD within Wise at a low fee → transfer CAD to a Canadian bank.

lessons.name: 105f9fc8
lessons.title: 2026 Roadmap Update + Q&A - January 21st, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A on e-commerce strategy, creative, and operations.
Key TakeawaysEvolve Community Shift: Evolve is moving from an info-hub to a high-performance community. It shifts beliefs and builds relatability, which is critical for scaling brands without a "show mechanism" (e.g., supplements, skincare).TopicsEvolve Community & Morocco EventCommunity Evolution: Evolve is shifting from an information-based community to a high-performance network.Morocco Event (Tickets Live): A break-even event designed for high value.
Speakers: Two confirmed guests (one on winning ads, one on building a real business), plus Spencer, Sean, and Zach Caria.Format: Day 1 → Speaker sessions; Day 2 → Action-oriented workshops in revenue-based groups.Awards: Custom awards for members who have hit $100k/day.Merch: Includes a custom-designed hat.Creative Strategy & ExecutionVideo vs. Static Performance:

Process: Identify the core angle, research why it resonates, then execute it in new ways (e.g., a story-based version of a comparison ad).Focus: The hook is the most critical element. It sets up the entire ad and is often the source of performance issues.Top-Performing Ad Formats:

lessons.name: 6e7826b3
lessons.title: Valence & Intensity - January 14th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeCall Starts: 2:00
To introduce the Valence & Intensity framework for creating more effective ad variations.
Key TakeawaysValence & Intensity (V&I) Framework: A psychological tool for creating ad variations by mapping copy to four emotional quadrants: Calm (high V, low I), Thrill (high V, high I), Annoyance (low V, low I), and Fear (low V, high I).Identify Your Winning Zone: Use AI (Claude/Gemini) to analyze winning ad hooks and find their V&I zone. This reveals the emotional tone that resonates most with your audience.Iterate Within & Across Zones: First, create more ads in your winning zone. Then, test the same angle in different V&I zones to find new scale opportunities.Ethical Use of Fear: The "Fear" zone (low V, high I) is powerful but requires extreme caution to avoid unethical fear-mongering, which leads to bans and brand damage.TopicsThe Valence & Intensity FrameworkCore Principle: Ad effectiveness is driven by how copy makes a customer feel, not just the words themselves.Valence: The emotional direction (positive vs. negative).Intensity: The emotional strength (calm vs. thrilled).The Four Quadrants:
Zone 1 (High V, Low I): Calm, Supportive
For defeated audiences needing reassurance.Example: "It's going to be okay."Zone 2 (High V, High I): Thrill, Excitement
For passionate audiences with a strong identity.Example: "This is your thing!"Zone 3 (Low V, Low I): Annoyance, Disappointment
For audiences frustrated by a common problem.Example: "Don't you hate it when..."Zone 4 (Low V, High I): Fear, Alarm
Taps into the subconscious survival instinct.Example: "Watch out for these ingredients..."Ad Journey: Ads must start in any zone but always end in a high-valence state to motivate purchase.Applying the V&I FrameworkProcess for Iteration:
Analyze Winners: Use AI to find the V&I zone of your top-performing ad hooks.Create More in Zone: Develop new ads that replicate the winning emotional tone.Test Across Zones: Apply the winning angle to different V&I zones to find new scale.Revive Old Angles: Re-test past winners by adapting them to your current winning zone.Ethical Considerations:
Rule: Do not fear-monger or lie.Guideline: Use verifiable facts (e.g., "ignoring this could lead to permanent damage").Best Practice: Use authentic, intense testimonials from customer stories.General Q&ASub-Avatar Testing:
Product Page: Keep the page generic, focusing on the core desire fulfilled by the product. The ad does the heavy lifting.Ad Copy: Use simple, broad body copy that works with any hook.Champions Ad Set:
Purpose: Protect proven winners from budget starvation by new ads.Method: Duplicate a winning ad into a separate "Champions" CBO campaign.Scaling Tactic: For high spend, create a "Winners ABO" campaign. Each winning ad gets its own ad set with a dedicated budget, forcing consistent spend.Low Budget Testing ($500/day):
Problem: Limited budget prevents rapid testing.Solution 1 (Intentional): Launch one high-quality ad batch per day. Review after 7 days and kill under performers.Solution 2 (Shotgun): Create a separate "raw content" campaign with a small budget ($100/day) to test many ads quickly.Unaware Audience Ads:
Goal: Capture broad attention before introducing the problem.Method: Start with a hook anyone can watch (e.g., juxtaposition, curiosity), then strategically bridge to the product.SEPA Payment Chargebacks:
Problem: High chargeback rate (5-6%) on recurring SEPA payments in the Netherlands/Belgium.Cause: Customers can easily reverse payments without contacting the merchant.Solution: Make the subscription nature extremely clear upfront (on-site, in emails) to prevent customer confusion.

lessons.name: 4c83e96b
lessons.title: How to write open Loops + Q&A - January 7th, 2026
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeWeekly Q&A and a tactical lesson on writing effective open loops for ads.
Key TakeawaysWrite Open Loops to Maintain Attention: Use Juxtaposition, Fear, and Contrarian angles to create curiosity gaps that maintain attention, targeting 90% retention at 6 seconds.Scale Smartly at $250k/Day: At high volume, prioritize backend stability (legal, compliance, supply chain) over aggressive growth to prevent catastrophic issues like lawsuits or payment processor holds.Brand Your Winners: A $300k/mo dropshipping store with a 30% return rate is a signal to brand the hero product. Use customer surveys to guide product development and secure credit terms with manufacturers.Evolve Event in Marrakech: The annual event is set for mid-to-late April in Marrakech, Morocco, and will be capped at 100 attendees on a first-come, first-served basis.TopicsEvolve Updates & Community NewsCopywriting Program: New modules will be released "Netflix-style," with potential live deep-dives on specific topics.Travel: Spencer and Sean will be in Italy and Dubai (for Agency Founders) in January.London Meetup: 28 members are attending a meetup organized by Wei Shaun Eng.Tactical Lesson: Writing Open Loops for AdsGoal: Maintain attention, not just grab it. The target is 90% retention at 6 seconds.Method 1: Juxtaposition
Pair two things that shouldn't go together to create a curiosity gap.Example: "I quit the gym and lost 20 pounds."Exercise: Practice with random concepts (e.g., "pour water in my gas tank") to train creative thinking.Method 2: Curiosity Through Fear
Leverage the brain's danger-detection instinct. "Sticks" are often more effective than "carrots."Example: "Watch out for these ingredients when buying shampoo."Note: This is not clickbait if the ad delivers on its promise and ethically connects to the product as a solution.Method 3: Do the Opposite
Stand out by directly contrasting industry norms.Example: Liquid Death's "grandma drinking water" ad vs. the typical "fancy model" ads from competitors.Broad-to-Niche Strategy
Start with a broad hook to capture wide attention.Funnel down by introducing specific avatar details later in the video.Rationale: This is more scalable than calling out a niche avatar immediately.Q&A: Scaling & StrategyProblem: Fake DMCA Takedowns at $250k/Day
Solution: Apply for Facebook's Brand Rights Protection Program. This requires a trademark and allows Facebook to automatically remove infringing ads.Problem: Scaling Stalled at $10k/Day Spend
Diagnosis: The current sub-avatar is saturated, causing frequency to rise.Solutions:
Broaden the Hook: Use a broad hook and funnel down to the sub-avatar.Test New Concepts: Dedicate a separate campaign to test new sub-avatars and angles.Refine Current Angle: Improve existing ads to push the current sub-avatar further.Problem: Post-Q4 Sales Dip for Seasonal Brand
Context: A watch accessory brand's ad spend dropped from $20k/day to $5k/day after the gifting season.Solution: Pivot Q1 messaging to focus on status and self-improvement. The dip is likely seasonal, and sales should rebound around Valentine's Day.Problem: Transitioning from Dropshipping to a Brand
Context: A dropshipping store earns $300k/mo but has a 30% return rate.Solution: Brand the store.
Survey Customers: Identify the hero product and what customers value.Improve Product: Work with manufacturers to enhance the hero product based on feedback.Secure Credit Terms: Negotiate credit terms (e.g., 30% upfront, 70% in 30 days) to protect cash flow.Problem: Deciding Between Two Brands
Context: A dropshipping brand with copyright issues is unprofitable. A new brand is launching on TikTok Shop and Amazon.Solution: If the old brand is unprofitable and a distraction, shut it down to focus fully on the new venture.

lessons.name: 55a88551
lessons.title: Copywriting Sneak Peek + Q&A - December 17th, 2025
lessons.description:
Meeting PurposeReview new tools and provide Q&A on ad strategy.
Key TakeawaysNew Discord AI Bot: "Chatbot" launches this week. It scrapes Evolve School and Discord history for instant answers, reducing wait times and improving information access.Copywriting Program Sneak Peek: A new program, included with Evolve, will teach the why behind effective copy, moving beyond generic AI prompts to build a core skill for scaling.Creative is the Bottleneck: Creative quality, not media buying strategy, is the primary barrier to scale. Ads must be strong enough to convert "colder" audiences as budgets increase.Testing Strategy: Test new ads directly in the main scaling campaign. Ads that fail to get spend there are not true winners and will likely underperform when forced into a larger budget.TopicsNew Discord AI Bot: ChatbotLaunch: Live in Discord by the end of this week.Function: Scrapes Evolve School and Discord history for instant answers to member questions.Benefit: Provides immediate, accurate responses, reducing reliance on staff and improving information access.Features:
Response time: <1 minute (necessary for accuracy).Source links: View original School or Discord content for context.Tagging: Tag the bot in any channel to get a response.Beta Test: May start in a dedicated #chatbot channel.Copywriting Program Sneak PeekGoal: Teach the why behind effective copy to build a core skill, moving beyond generic AI prompts.Status: Included with Evolve membership; not an upsell.Content Overview:
Fundamentals: Pattern recognition, visual writing, positioning (e.g., the "DNA test that tells you when you'll die").Strategies: Hooks, open loops, raising stakes, handling objections, storytelling.Tools: Milanote for visual layout, power words, etc.Examples: Spencer will write winning ads for various niches (starting with Apex members).Timeline: Modules will be released "Netflix-style" starting Q1 2026.Q&A: Ad Strategy & ScalingTesting in New Accounts:
Budget: Use a minimum of $100/day to allow Meta enough data to find a purchase.Action: Turn off ads that spend ~8x target CPA with no conversions. This helps Meta learn faster in a data-poor environment.Camouflage Ads (Long-Form Image):
Format: Image ad with a long, story-driven copy block.Effectiveness: Works well for older demographics (45+) who prefer reading.Landing Page: Test with a product page first to validate the concept before investing in a custom advertorial.Campaign Structure & Scaling:
Problem: A structure with many CBOs and no ad turn-offs can lead to performance instability.Root Cause: Ads are not strong enough to convert "colder" audiences as budgets increase.Solution: Focus on improving creative quality. If the current structure is working, commit to it and prioritize creative development.Testing in a Scaling Campaign:
Problem: Ads tested in a small, separate campaign often fail in the main scaling campaign.Reason: Forcing spend in a small campaign creates false positives by targeting low-hanging fruit. The main campaign's algorithm correctly identifies these as weak ads.Solution: Test new ads directly in the main scaling campaign. If an ad doesn't get spend, it's not a true winner.Doubling Down on a Winning Persona:
Method: Expand creative angles for the persona by targeting different "selves" (ideal, ought, actual) and testing new formats (VSLs, podcasts, storytelling).

We only run this type of campaigns during sale periods. Mother's Day, BFCM, etc.
1 CBO campaign
3 Ad sets total

1 Broad ad set
1 WARM60 ad set - FB Engagers, IG Engagers, 95% Video Viewers over the last 60 days
1 HOT90 ad set - Website visitors, view content, add to cart, initiate checkout over last 90 days

For the ads just put sale banners over existing best ads, and introduce some simple product image ads that mention the sale.

Keep it simple.

We usually don't do retargeting but the only time we do is during a sale. Having 3 ad sets like this in a CBO means FB will spend on wherever it thinks will do the best.

lessons.name: 7cbf5f4b
lessons.title: Dubai Mastermind Recording
lessons.description:
Introduction and Purpose of the Mastermind• Timestamps: 00:00:00 --> 00:00:49
Summary: The event, initially planned as a dinner meetup, evolved into a mastermind
session. Attendees include individuals ranging from seven-figure to eight-figure
monthly earners. The primary goal is for everyone to connect, mingle, and collectively
solve problems they face in their businesses.
Participant Introductions and Key Challenges• Timestamps: 00:01:27 --> 00:13:31
Discussion on Team Building and Hiring• Timestamps: 00:13:48 - 00:56:32
Summary: The main speaker (Spencer) and Shaun discuss best practices for team
building, emphasizing the importance of hiring the right people (not out of
desperation), and the two ways to build teams: bottom-up (common, starting with
junior roles) and top-down (hiring strategists/leaders first).
They stress the difficulty of finding good creative strategists and suggest either headhunting experienced individuals or hiring driven individuals and training them using their program.
They highlight the importance of clear expectations, KPIs, and investing time in developing
team members.
They also discuss how to retain talent through vision, culture, and fair compensation, noting that money isn't the only motivator.
The interview process, including loom videos, initial screenings, assessments, and reference checks, is detailed.
They also touch on the importance of continuous recruiting and being prepared to replace underperforming team members.
The discussion includes how to handle team members who are not improving and the importance of open communication and performance improvement plans.
Discussion on Incentives and Compensation• Timestamps: 00:56:32 - 01:12:28
Summary: The conversation shifts to incentivizing creative teams.
They discuss various models, including flat bonuses per winning ad, rolling percentages of ad spend, and cash bonuses based on overall business revenue goals.
The key is to make incentives clear, tangible, and aligned with company goals.
They emphasize that incentives should be a win-win for both the company and the employee.
They also discuss how non-monetary incentives like job titles, growth opportunities, and appreciation can be powerful motivators.
The example of an operations manager whose pay is scaled based on revenue is given to illustrate how to incentivize roles that don't directly generate revenue but are crucial for the company's smooth operation.
Content Creators and Affiliates• Timestamps: 01:16:31 - 01:42:51
Summary: The discussion moves to content creators and affiliates, particularly in the
context of UGC (User-Generated Content) and TikTok Shop.
They highlight that creators can act as strategists, copywriters, filmers, and editors all in one, and that UGC often yields better results than traditional ads.
They explain their strategy of product seeding and then hiring creators who produce winning ads on a retainer, with additional incentives based on ad spend or revenue.
The idea of using coupon codes for affiliates to automate payments and track performance is also explored.
They emphasize that the goal is to generate content that can be used for paid ads, effectively making money while acquiring content.
The importance of white-listing access for creators is mentioned.
The conversation also touches on the difference between UGC creators and traditional influencers, and how to leverage both for different purposes, with a focus on performance over follower count.
They discuss how to get creators to produce content by providing clear guidelines, hooks, and b-roll examples, while also allowing them creative freedom.
The concept of using TikTok Shop as a content generation engine, even if direct sales from it are not the primary goal, is also discussed.

lessons.name: 522473f8
lessons.title: Why the fact it’s hard is actually good
lessons.description:
If something were easy, everyone would have it. Difficulty is a filter that separates those who want it from those who deserve it.The “hardness” of something is what creates scarcity. Scarcity = value.“The fact that most people quit is the reason you shouldn’t.”
- Someone smarter than meEmotional FramingEvery frustration (No winning ads, low ROAS, losing money) is proof that you’re in the arena. Most aren’t.Instead of saying “this is hard,” say: “This is the part that makes it worth it.”
That mindset flips pain into proof of progress.The very reason most people don’t have it, is the same reason it’s so rewarding when you finally do.The fact that it’s hard is what makes it worth it.
- Mozi
...Also, it’s not really that hard lol...

🕰️ Then vs. Now — “Starting a Business in the 1990s vs. 2020s”THEN (1990s)
Had to rent office space — even if you were solo.Needed landlines, fax machines, and physical business cards.Building a website? Cost $10K–$50K and took months.Marketing? Yellow Pages, newspaper ads, or local radio.To reach customers outside your city, you needed a warehouse, shipping partners, and trust built through mail-order catalogs.To hire? You posted in local classifieds. Couldn’t tap into global talent.Raising money meant begging banks or investors for a loan and wearing a suit.Scaling beyond your town required logistics, not just clicks.NOW (2020s+)
You can start a brand from your couch with $1,000 and a laptop.No-code tools (Shopify, Webflow, Zapier) let you launch a full business in a day.You can test ideas with AI, market research, ad copy, product names, instantly.You can hire people from the Philippines, Pakistan, or Eastern Europe for a fraction of local cost.You can reach 10,000,000 people overnight with one viral video or ad for FREE.You can receive instant feedback from comments, analytics, or surveys.You can sell globally, automatic translations, global payment processors, fulfillment handled by Amazon or 3PLs.You can learn everything for free on YouTube, X, or inside communities like Origins for less than $100.You can literally talk to an AI team 24/7 to help you brainstorm, design, and execute.In 1995, if you wanted to start a supplement brand, you’d need to convince a manufacturer to take your call, spend $30K on product runs, $10K on design, and pray you could get your product into local stores.
In 2025, you can get a Shopify template, prompt Claude for your product description, hire a designer on Fiverr, and run your first ad on Meta all before lunch.💡 Data & Historical ExamplesAmazon took three years to hit $1M/month in revenue.
→ Many Shopify stores hit that in less than 6 months today.Nike’s first ad in the ‘70s cost $10,000 and reached thousands.
→ A single UGC video can reach millions organically.Hiring developers in 1995: $80K+ salary, on-site.
→ Hiring developers in 2025: $2K/month, remote from anywhere.

lessons.title: Live Product Research w/ Kalodata - Pt 2
lessons.description:
Note:
To clarify, this does not mean you should rip ads and hope for the best. You have to make your own ads together based on the following modules. If you don't figure out how to stand out beforehand and create your own ads to do so, you will not build any skills.

Checklist from the video:
1) For this method we're using a paid tool Kalodata. Kalodata is a tool that pulls the best performing TikTok shop products. You can get access to it for cheaper via Toolsuite
2) Filter at the product level. Last 7 days, Avg unit price >$15, sales growing rapidly.
3) Any of the products here not attached to a big brand (E.g. Goli, Shark, Comfrt) has the potential to be sold.
4) Go through the listings and look into the brand to verify if it is a big brand. Do a Google search, check their social media following. If they're a established brand they can easily afford litigation to take you down. Not worth it running bootleg versions.

5) Check the trademark websites on wherever you plan to sell to verify if the brand/product name has a trademark. For example in the US you may use https://tmsearch.uspto.gov/search/search-information (Free) or GPT/Claude to find out. If the product is called "Blood Elixir" and all the TT videos mention it, if you reuse those clips with product name mention there's a higher risk of getting taken down. In that case obviously use a different brand name and also different product name. Trademarked doesn't mean you can't sell the product, just means you can't use certain phrases on the site and ads.
6) Use Similarweb (via Toolsuite) to estimate how much the store is doing. Always be more conservative. Let's say the average is 1% conversion rate (CVR). Estimate the AOV based on product selling price. Website visitors x CVR x AOV = Estimated Revenue. For this prod research method, the estimated revenue on the site is less important as some stores do a lot with TTS but not on their own website. Product can still sell via FB ads.
7) Do some basic research on the product. Go through the top performing videos from Kalodata TikTok shop videos and the comments. See what's the current angle they're targeting, who they're targeting, what the comments are saying.

8) Also go through https://www.facebook.com/ads/library and Atria (via Toolsuite) to see what the competition is running.

9) Do more research based on the subsequent modules on how to find your avatar. Wherever possible - Google search, YT videos, IG reels, Tiktok videos. We know there's only 2 ways to win if you're not first to market. A new mechanism or an underserved avatar. The subsequent module will cover the avatar side. Our goal with this research is to find if we can find new angles, mechanisms, or avatars we can target besides what the competition is doing so you can stand out. So we need to know what types of angles your current competition is running and the current market sophistication level.

10) Check with the supplier (supplier here) if the pricing they can get makes sense. You want to use tools like Claude, GPT or Amazon to check what is the average price for the product you're going to sell so it's reasonable and within expectation. If you're selling super premium prices but only sell cheap low quality products it won't go well. After getting a quote or checking on AliExpress, see if you 3x'd the COGS (cost of goods) + Shipping, if the product still falls under the expected price range. E.g. $20 COGs total, $60 selling price, $40-60 is expected price based on Claude/Amazon.

11) After you found a potential product, you will create your own creatives based on research, alongside the top 10-20 best-performing (by revenue) videos that Kalodata shows. How to create the creatives is a module later in the course.

Note:
For brand new beginners, I do not recommend starting out with a higher ticket item like the 1st product in the video at $100+ product price. Starting out, finding products you can sell for $40-80 is good

And also, you can't rely on the ripped creatives to scale long term. Treat it as borrowed time. It's only a matter of time until it dies or gets taken down, even though the store has traction now treat it with urgency. Now you're profitable while trying to figure out how to create your own winning creatives that stand out.

lessons.title: 🆕 How to feel better about being overwhelmed
lessons.description:
First, what is the definition?
Definition: 
Bury or drown beneath a huge mass.
Our Definition:
Give too much of a thing to (someone);
Story: (AF 2024)
Clickup Notes
What You Have To Do:
Study → Research → Create → Test → Feedback Loop → RepeatStudy: Learning new information to build your knowledge basis
Research: Figure out what people want
Create: Communicate how you can help those people get what they want
Test: Launch tests in 1 campaign. If it gets spend = good. If it does not get spend = not good.
Feedback Loop: Make educated guesses on why your ad is working or not working
Repeat: Go back to researching again, or leverage learnings from the feedback loop to make more.
That's It.

Words I Live By:
This system is exactly how you're going to get to 100k/month and exactly how others get to 100k/day

lessons.title: Understanding ad definitions
lessons.description:
Defintions:
💻3:2:2 ⇒ 3 creatives, 2 body copies, and 2 headlines
12-Year-Old Definition: The testing structure we use inside of Meta. 
Example:
This ENTIRE thing is a Concept. “3” = Variations of that 1 Concept. 
“2:2” = 2 Headline + 2 Body copy for that Concept that you put inside of Meta.


📂Concept/Batch/Test #:⇒ The tracking number for this test
12-Year-Old Definition: The number you use to keep track of which test you're on
Examples: 
Batch #1, Batch #29, Batch #133
💡Concept/Swing ⇒ The test strategy - what you're testing in this batch
12-Year-Old Concept Definition: The big idea behind the ads you want to test
Examples: 
"Test an iteration on a winning video."
"Test superlative angles."
"Test UGC format"
"Test different avatars."

🔗Angle⇒The selling strategy - how you're choosing to sell the product
12-Year-Old Angle Definition: The main reason you're giving someone to buy 
Examples:
"Buy It For Life"
"Postpartum weight despite trying everything"
"Stainless steel / Doctor-designed / Cleanest"
Key insight: Every ad needs an angle. Even if your concept is "testing formats," you still need to define what you're selling. If your concept is “Testing X Angle” the concept becomes the angle. But for tracking purposes, I prefer to actually JOT DOWN the angle twice so we can be sure.


🔀Variations ⇒ Individual executions of the angle(s)
12-Year-Old Variations Definition: Different ways to communicate your selling reason(s)
Example: 
If your angle is "Buy It For Life," variations might be: "One harness, lifetime of adventures," "Buy it once, adventure for life," or "End the replacement cycle"
If testing multiple angles, variations might be different angles like "Stainless steel," "Doctor-designed," "Easiest to clean."


🖼️Format ⇒ How you deliver the ad
12-Year-Old Format Definition: The type of ad you're making
Example: You could show the same message as a video of a real person talking, a slideshow of pictures, or just a product image.

lessons.title: How to create image ads - part 2
lessons.description:
0:00 - Research + Flow
In the first part of the video, I talk about the importance of research, how to do more research for sub-avatars to get more ideas, as well as the importance of not just restricting yourself to JUST research. It's important that if you have a creative idea for writing, you can just start writing it.
9:04 - Image First Training
Image firsts approach --> Sourcing Image styles FIRST, putting into Claude, and having it replicate the ads for you.
39:50 - Reviewing Part 1 Designs
 at this point, we start to review the images that I made in part 1, the module above this to talk about the Pro Tip linked below.
44:40 - Answer FAQs Below
46:30 - Making a Congruent Image With Nano Banana AI

⭐️ Pro Tip:
Rather than making more ads after a break, just optimize the existing ads you previously made. Give your brain SPACE to marinate ideas and come back with fresh eyes.
Tools I Used In The Video:
Creative OS:
https://www.creativeos.com/

Nano Banana:
https://aistudio.google.com/
FAQs:
Are those big enough swings if you use the same template?
Yes.
Can you test different visuals (Like the Carepod method)?
Yes.. But I would only recommend it if you have a graphic designer who can make congruent ads
Final Ads From Part 2:

How many creative ad sets can you launch at a time?
If you're only spending few hundred a day, I recommend keeping it to 5 ad sets (including champions ad set, if it has ads inside) at a time so budget can be distributed efficiently. Total Ads = Budget/TCPA

lessons.name: 9f47172b
lessons.title: Extra FAQ for Product Testing
lessons.description:
1) Is there a special campaign you use for product testing?
No, it's still the same broad 1 CBO campaign as shown in the video above
2) How long do you test a product for before moving on?
The answer to this depends on your skill level. If you're a complete beginner, it's much better to test a product for 3 days, and if there's no traction (your goal is to get something to breakeven) then you can move on to the next product.
This way, you take more "Medium intent" swings rather than going high intent and low volume. At the beginning stages, you need volume, because you don't know what good and bad looks like yet. You will build up your skills faster this way.
If you try to make everything perfect before launching, it takes too much time, and the extra time you spent could be trash too, since you don't know what good and bad looks like.
If you're more experienced and trying to start a new E-Commerce brand now, you can test it for 1-2 weeks while continually adding new ads to test. Since we know you can make any product work, it might just take 1 winning ad in that period to turn things around.
3) Should I touch the ads or kill products early based on the metrics?

People will tell you they kill based on CTR, CPC, cost per add to cart, etc
I don't really care about any of that. All I care about is spend and ROAS. Because if you have an ad that gets only $0.01 spend but has a high CTR, it's still a bad ad.
The goal is to have your product break even during the initial test. If it's at least breakeven,n it means you can invest in improving things to make it profitable and scale now.
Continue testing for the 3 days and see if the product has traction or not; don't need to turn off any ads until then.
